paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.39:1 Rule 5.39 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.39. 1. Expert Reports To Be Entered Into Court Record Only On Consent or Order In Henderson (Estate) v. Arnett, 2011 ABQB 198, 2011 CarswellAlta 471, 50 Alta. L.R. (5th) 40, Justice Binder heard an application by the Defendants in a medical malpractice action for an order directing the removal from the court file seven expert Substances of Opinion which had been filed by the Plaintiff. Binder, J. noted at paragraph 2; 2 The Plaintiffs (Respondents) filed the Substances of Opinion in 2009 and served the same reports upon counsel for the Defendants, pursuant to Rule 218.1(1) of the old Alberta Rules of Court. They intend to call the authors of these reports as witnesses at trial, and therefore have not filed Notices pursuant to Rule 218.1(2) of the old Alberta Rules of Court or Rule 5.39(1) of the new Alberta Rules of Court. In granting the application, Binder, J. said, at paragraphs 8–15: 8 Rule 1.2 sets out the purpose and intention of the Rules, including to identify the real issues in dispute, facilitate the quickest means of resolving a claim at the least expense, encourage the parties to resolve the claim themselves as early in the process as practicable, and oblige the parties to communicate honestly, openly and in a timely way. Parties are to refrain from filing applications or taking proceedings that do not further the purpose and intention of these rules, and are to use publicly funded court resources effectively. 9 Rule 5.32, under Division 1—How Information Is Disclosed, provides that documents under Division 1 must not be filed. These include the transcript of questioning, including exhibits, an affidavit of records, affidavits and answers to written questions, and correcting affidavits. They are not be put before the court except during an application, proceeding or at trial, and may be filed and put before the court only as permitted by the Rules. 10 Old Rule 212(4) also prohibited filing the examination for discovery transcript. This position reflects the fact that discovery is a private process, and that invasion of privacy should generally be limited to the level of disclosure necessary to satisfy that purpose of the civil action: Juman v. Doucette, 2008 SCC 8, [2008] 1 S.C.R. 157. 11 It is interesting to note that the Alberta Law Reform Institute in its Documentary Discovery and Examination for Discovery—Consultation Memorandum No. 12.2 at paras. 44 and 45 considered whether the affidavit of records must be filed with the clerk, noting that the affidavit of records is rarely in issue, and filing it simply results in a waste of scarce storage space. The ALRI recommended that it not be filed unless an issue arises as to its contents. 12 Rules 5.34 to 5.40, in Division 2—Experts and Expert Reports deal with expert reports. They contemplate service between parties, but no mention is made of filing such reports with the court. 13 Finally, in Division 4—Filed Documents, Subdivision 2—Form and Contents of Affidavits and Exhibits, Rule 13.26 refers to exhibits “filed with the court clerk in a hearing or trial”. 14 In my view, the new Rules reflect a policy of efficiency and economy. Restricting filing to essentials promotes those goals. Unnecessary filing wastes court resources in terms of clerk's time and storage space. Counsel should communicate honestly, openly and in a timely way amongst themselves. Expert reports should only become part of the court record by consent or with the approval of the court. Counsel should advise the trial coordinators of the names of the experts at the time of setting down the matter for trial, in order to avoid conflicts between experts and the judge hearing the matter. Conclusion 15 Expert reports should only become part of the court record by consent or with the approval of the court. Accordingly, the Court grants an order to remove the Substances of Opinion from the court file. In Campbell v. Beekman, 2011 ABQB 437, 2011 CarswellAlta 1165, 523 A.R. 133, 55 Alta. L.R. (5th) 280, Lee, J. referred with approval to Henderson (Estate) v. Arnett, and said, at paragraph 6: 6 The Rules are essentially silent with respect to the unfiling of Expert Reports, but the Court has the general discretion to unfile, which it may exercise in appropriate circumstances. Given that the issue is non-contentious at least with respect to the unfiling of the present report of Dr. Nicholas Colapinto filed on September 21, 2010, I will allow the application, and not award costs to either party for the application. 2. Entering Report in Absence of Expert As to when leave should be granted: These examples of the flagrant ignoring of the provisions of rule 218.1 present an opportunity for the purpose of the rule to be restated, together with duties of counsel thereunder, as well as an articulation of a standard as to whom leave should be granted under rule 218.1(2). I also note, in passing, that there is no authority to relieve from a failure to comply with 218.1(3)—that is, a party calling an expert witness (even where there is compliance with the other parts of rule 218.1) “shall” serve any report intended to be filed as part of the expert's evidence not less than 10 days prior to the commencement of the trial. In my view, before leave should be granted by the court pursuant to rule 218.1(2), more than just prejudice to counsel for the opposite party in terms of cross-examination needs to be considered. The whole purpose of the rule needs to be considered. The case of Commonwealth Construction Co. Ltd. v. Syncrude Canada Ltd. ((1985), 40 Alta. L.R. (2d) 89 (Q.B.)—Purvis, J.), appears to be the first case in Alberta to consider the rule originally brought in under Alta. Reg. 66/85. That case was concerned primarily with the issue of what constituted the “substance of his opinion” in rule 218.1(1). The court, in simple terms, held that “substance” means the facts upon which the opinions are based, as well as the opinions themselves. However, in the process of examining the issue of substance, the purpose of the rule was also examined. Purvis, J., applied the rules of interpretation to determine the meaning of the word “substance” but these rules, the necessary changes being made, apply in principle to not only the interpretation of the words themselves but the interpretation of the intent behind the rule. Firstly, Purvis, J., applied the “Mischief Rule” saying: “The court should then interpret the statute in a way that will suppress the mischief and advance the remedy.” He also applied the “Remedial Legislation Rule” in these words: “It is also a rule of statutory interpretation that remedial legislation should be construed liberally to achieve the remedy”. He further stated: “With these guides [Mischief Rule and Remedial Legislation Rule] in mind, I propose to accord to rule 218.1(1) a large and liberal interpretation”. He then identified the “Mischief to be suppressed and the remedy effected by the Rule”: The Rule was formulated for the purpose of preventing disruption of the trial process which occurs when litigants are taken by surprise. If the parties know ahead of time what expert opinions they will encounter they can adjust to meet the evidence without asking for adjournment. In some cases settlement may be encouraged. In any event, costs and time will be saved and the judicial process will be simplified if there is full disclosure. In referring to the authorities therein set out, he identified (by quotes from those authorities) further purposes of the rule, which include the following: • save expense by dispensing with the calling of experts when there is really no dispute (which can only be determined after examining the substance of their opinion); • the possibility of avoiding amendment of pleadings; • the saving of costs and expense; • preparation on the basis of knowledge of the case to be met; • to settle issue within the trial; • shorten trials; and • to enable the experts themselves to prepare their evidence more thoroughly and helpfully. One other reason and purpose for the rule would relate to the retaining of rebuttal experts to provide advice for cross-examination or to provide a report or both. In the latter case, opposite counsel must also comply with rule 218.1(1). There are undoubtedly other reasons and purposes. Thus, one can see the mere absence of prejudice to the opposite party in terms of trying to prepare cross-examination is not, in most cases, a sufficient basis for the court to grant leave under rule 218.1(2) … In the case of Wilson v. Walton et al. (No. 1) (1987), 79 A.R. 97 (Q.B.), Waite, J., considered the rule as an absolute rule, unless there was some satisfactory explanation. I agree with that categorization. In giving his judgment, he said this (at 99): There has been in this case in my judgment no satisfactory explanation offered as to why the Rule was not substantially complied with. I would not in this case consider granting leave without at least an adjournment to the defendant. There are two objections to doing so [granting leave]. The first is that this cause of action arose some seven years ago and the action itself was commenced some five years ago. … There has been one trial adjournment. In the circumstances mentioned there ought not to be another. The second complication is the fact that this trial has now started and I am now seized with the trial whether it continues now or at some future time. I am satisfied there has been noncompliance. I am satisfied that no satisfactory reason exists why leave of the court should be granted pursuant to the Rule. The consequence is that the expert shall not testify. … In Alberta Motor Association Insurance Co. v. Lenzo (1990), 74 Alta. L.R. (2d) 218, the Court of Appeal dismissed an appeal from this court which denied an application under rule 218.1(2), stating (at 219): The purpose of r. 218 is to ensure that the parties be prepared for trial, and this requires early notice of expert evidence. In fact, notice was given here … late by any standard, and particularly in the circumstances here … The circumstances included the jury trial date being adjourned for four plus months for the specific purpose of re-organizing expert testimony. The court went on to allow leave to renew the application before the trial judge if there could be more substantial compliance, stating: R. 218.1 of course gives the court authority to grant leave to call a witness late. In our view, leave should be granted in a case where late notice remains adequate notice in terms of preparation. Wherever possible it is best that the trier of fact hear all relevant evidence. But that ideal must be tempered by the recognition that we must have a workable system. In conclusion, these cases make it clear that, while there may be relief from the strict requirement of rule 218.1, such relief will be very sparingly granted. Guarantee Co. of North America v. Beasse (1992), 124 A.R. 161 (Q.B.), at 229-31, per Rooke J.

paragraphs.text: 5.40. Expert's attendance at trial
paragraphs.heading: Part 5. Disclosure Of Information

sentences.text: Expert's attendance at trial

paragraphs.text: (1) A party who agrees to have all of an expert's report entered in evidence at trial, either explicitly or by allowing rule 5.39(2) to operate without objection, may, at the same time as responding to the notice of intention, serve a request that the expert be in attendance at trial for cross-examination. (2) The expert whose entire report is to be entered at trial must not give oral evidence at trial unless (a) a request that the expert attend for cross-examination has been served, or (b) the Court permits. (3) The party who requests an expert's attendance for cross-examination must pay the costs of the expert's attendance, determined under Schedule B, unless the Court is satisfied that the cross-examination is of sufficient assistance to warrant a different order about who is to pay those costs. (4) If the party proposing to enter the expert's report receives a request that the expert attend for cross-examination, the party proposing to enter the report may question the expert at trial.

(2) The expert whose entire report is to be entered at trial must not give oral evidence at trial unless (a) a request that the expert attend for cross-examination has been served, or (b) the Court permits.

(3) The party who requests an expert's attendance for cross-examination must pay the costs of the expert's attendance, determined under Schedule B, unless the Court is satisfied that the cross-examination is of sufficient assistance to warrant a different order about who is to pay those costs.
(4) If the party proposing to enter the expert's report receives a request that the expert attend for cross-examination, the party proposing to enter the report may question the expert at trial.

paragraphs.text: 5.41. Medical examinations
paragraphs.heading: Part 5. Disclosure Of Information

sentences.text: Medical examinations

paragraphs.text: (1) The parties may agree that the mental or physical condition of a person is at issue in an action and agree on a health care professional to conduct a medical examination. (2) On application, the Court may in an action in which the mental or physical condition of a person is at issue do either or both of the following: (a) order that a person submit to a mental or physical medical examination; (b) appoint a health care professional to conduct a medical examination. (3) The Court may order a second or further medical examination by a health care professional. (4) If the plaintiff has been the subject of a medical examination by a health care professional of the plaintiff's choice who will or may be proffered as an expert, the Court may order that the plaintiff be the subject of a medical examination by one or more health care professionals of the defendant's choice.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.41:1 Rule 5.41 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.41. 1. Timing of the exchange of reports In Erketu v. Wilson, 2013 ABQB 247, 2013 CarswellAlta 534, 560 A.R. 260, 81 Alta. L.R. (5th) 35, Justice Nielsen considered this issue: “whether the Court should order that a defendant in a personal injury action make its position known on an ME under Rule 5.41 prior to the plaintiff disclosing its expert report(s) under Rule 5.35.” In holding that a defendant should not be so ordered, his Lordship said, at paragraphs 32–58: 32 There is no dispute that the expert reports sought by the Defendants are covered by litigation privilege. Litigation privilege attaches to documents that have been created for the dominant purpose of furthering litigation: Opron Construction Co v. Alberta (1989), 100 AR 58, 1989 ABCA 279 (Canlii). The purpose of litigation privilege is to create a zone of privacy in relation to pending or apprehended litigation by providing a protected area to facilitate investigation and preparation of a case for trial by the adversarial advocate: Blank v. Canada (Minister of Justice), 2006 SCC 39, [2006] 2 SCR 319 at para 34. The rationale for the privilege is that the adversarial system requires that each party be able to prepare its case in private: Pinder v. Sproule, 2003 ABQB 33, 333 AR 132 at para 48. 33 An expert report prepared in contemplation of litigation is clearly subject to litigation privilege, and the party who ordered the report is entitled to suppress its disclosure. Litigation privilege can be waived expressly or by knowingly providing a copy of the document to another party, or by attempting to rely on the privileged documents to obtain some relief from the Court: Pinder v. Sproule at para 10. Litigation privilege is waived when expert reports are used in Court. 34 Rule 5.35 is a statutory exception to litigation privilege. Unlike Former Rule 218.1, Rule 5.35 provides a sequential exchange of expert reports. It generally dictates that the party bearing the primary onus of proof must waive litigation privilege with respect to the expert report(s) upon which that party intends to rely. In a personal injury action, this results in a plaintiff waiving litigation privilege with respect to the expert report(s) it intends to adduce at trial. 35 Rule 5.44(3), like Former Rule 217(7), is another statutory exception to litigation privilege, relating specifically to medical-legal reports and reports of medical examinations sought by a defendant after an ME under Rule 5.41: Andre v. Wiebe, 2000 ABQB 946, 284 AR 378 at para 7. It does not result only in disclosure of the report(s) the plaintiff intends to adduce at trial, but, rather, disclosure of reports of every medical examination previously or subsequently made. 36 In my view, the question is not whether Rule 5.44(3) impinges on litigation privilege. Clearly, it does do so. If a defendant does not request an ME thereby triggering Rule 5.44(3), litigation privilege remains on any expert report which a plaintiff does not intend to adduce. 37 However, a plaintiff, in order to advance the action, must waive privilege on expert reports upon which it intends to rely, under Rule 5.35. 38 The Plaintiffs argue that the Rules contain a “gap” and the Court should require the Defendants to make a decision on an ME prior to the Plaintiffs disclosing under Rule 5.35. 39 In my view, there is no gap in the Rules. The Plaintiffs argue that the use of Rule 5.35 to obtain the Plaintiffs' medical expert reports without first conducting an ME would render Rule 5.44(3) useless. I do not agree. The two Rules can work in conjunction to provide the Court with the most complete evidence of a plaintiff's medical condition when that is at issue in litigation. 40 The onus is on a plaintiff to advance its action. Rule 5.35 generally reflects this onus in requiring the party with the onus to disclose first. 41 The real question is whether there is anything in the Rules which prevents a defendant from waiting to rely on Rules 5.41 and 5.44 until after a plaintiff has disclosed its expert report(s) under Rule 5.35. 42 In fact, there is nothing in the Rules that prevents a defendant from doing so. Nothing in the Rules dictates that steps pursuant to Rules 5.41 and 5.44 must occur before the plaintiff discloses pursuant to Rule 5.35. Although Rule 1.2(3) now mandates that all parties must facilitate the quickest means of resolving the claim at the least expense, nothing in the Rules requires a defendant to take any initiative under Rule 5.41 prior to the plaintiff's disclosure under Rule 5.35. It would have been a simple thing for the legislature to provide otherwise. 43 Rules 5.41(1) and 5.44(3), and Former Rule 217, have existed in relatively the same form since the 1968 Rules of Court as a mechanism for the defendant to have physical access to a plaintiff and to have disclosure of records of the plaintiff's previous medical examinations prior to trial. As explained by MacDonald J. in Petersen v. Shepard (1985), 58 AR 240, [1985] AJ No 651 at para 7 (QB), this was important because previously there was no rule which required the disclosure of expert reports prior to trial. If no ME was performed under Former Rule 217, a defendant could learn of an expert's evidence for the first time only at the actual trial. This procedure of keeping evidence hidden from the other party until trial was a system of “trial by ambush”. 44 This system of “trial by ambush” was altered in 1985 when Rule 5.35, in its original form of Former Rule 218.1, was introduced. Former Rule 218.1(1) became another limit on “trial by ambush” since it abolished the litigation privilege on expert reports by requiring disclosure prior to trial. The adoption of Former Rule 218.1 did not result in the abolition of Former Rule 217. 45 Rule 5.35 and Rules 5.41 to 5.44 serve different purposes. Rule 5.35 requires the disclosure of expert reports that will be relied on at trial. This allows a defendant to know the evidence the plaintiff will be relying on and provides an opportunity to counter the expert evidence. Rule 5.35 relates to the disclosure of any type of expert evidence in any type of litigation. 46 Rules 5.41 to 5.44 only relate to the medical evidence of a litigant's condition. Allowing a physical examination of a plaintiff and the disclosure of reports of previous medical examinations ensures that the court will have adequate evidence to assess a plaintiff's claim when it relates to a medical condition. The disclosure of reports of previous medical examinations allows a defendant to assess issues surrounding the cause, nature, or aggravation of the injuries. The unique nature of a claim for medical injuries requires unique rules. A party who has put his or her physical condition in issue should not be in a position to deny the opposite party the right to ascertain his or her physical condition by suitable examination by a medical practitioner: Jacobson v. Sveen, 2000 ABQB 215, 262 AR 367 at paras 42 and 43. Rule 5.44(3) is an additional type of disclosure of records and an additional exchange of expert reports. This provision has specific application only when an ME is conducted. Otherwise, Rule 5.35 governs the exchange of expert reports. 47 The Plaintiffs are concerned that if they are required to disclose their expert reports, the examiner who performs an ME may be biased by the information. Lefsrud J. came to this conclusion in Soodhar v. Bagley (1999), 263 AR 119, [1999] AJ No 1592 (QB). With respect, I reject this as supporting the withholding of the expert reports required to be disclosed under Rule 5.35. 48 An ME is a defendant's examination, not an independent examination. As stated by the Alberta Court of Appeal in Grayson v. Demers, [1975] 2 WWR 289, [1974] AJ No 291 (CA), “the medical practitioner who conducts an ME under rule 217 is clearly doing so on behalf of the person seeking the examination, in other words, the person against whom compensation or damages is sought”. 49 A medical professional performing an ME has an obligation to be objective and to provide an honest opinion. Seeing another expert's report does not, in and of itself, undermine an expert's opinion: Jacobson v. Sveen at paras 36 and 44. Further, potential bias created by the medical professional having access to the plaintiffs' medical reports prior to the ME can be assessed under cross-examination and determined by a trial judge: Rosario-Paquet v. Hudec, 2000 ABQB 762, 279 AR 319 at para 24. Trial judges are accustomed to assessing reliability and credibility and attributing appropriate weight to evidence. They are accustomed to assessing competing expert evidence. As a result, the potential for bias, without more, does not support the withholding of the Plaintiffs' expert reports until after the Defendants have moved under Rule 5.44(3). 50 I note in this regard that the Plaintiffs concede that subsequent MEs could be ordered by the Defendants after disclosure is triggered following the first ME, a position which is consistent with Veit J.'s decision in Jacobson v. Sveen. Any potential for bias would exist with respect to those subsequent MEs. 51 This approach is consistent with Rule 1.2. In particular, the Rules should be interpreted to facilitate the quickest means of resolving a claim at the least expense, and to oblige the parties to communicate honestly, openly and in a timely way. 52 This approach is also consistent with the purposes stated in Rule 5.1, in particular encouraging early disclosure of facts and records, facilitating evaluation of the parties' positions, and discouraging conduct that unnecessarily or improperly delays proceedings or unnecessarily increases the cost of them. 53 To rule otherwise would be to require defendants in such actions to potentially incur unnecessary costs to obtain the very disclosure to which they are entitled under Rule 5.35 and which they will receive in any event prior to the matter being set down for trial. 54 Unlike the Former Rules, the Rules no longer provide specific instructions regarding the timing of the exchange of expert reports. The only requirement is that the party bearing the onus of proof provide its reports first. This is a change from the specific deadlines set out in the Former Rules. The Rules allow the parties to determine their own timelines for the litigation process and the disclosure of expert reports. 55 Although the timelines from Former Rule 218.1 are not contained in Rule 5.35, the purpose of Rule 5.35 remains the same. It is designed to prevent one party from surprising the other with expert testimony. The emphasis is on a fair and workable process for disclosure: Stewart Estate v. TAQA North Ltd., 2012 ABQB 87, [2012] AJ No 188 at para 19. It requires parties to give notice of their expert evidence and to waive litigation privilege in time to allow the other side to know the case he or she has to meet and to allow a reasonable chance to respond. As stated by Slatter J., as he then was, “It allows the experts to focus on what is truly in dispute. The rule was never intended to be a chess game between counsel”: Wade v. Baxter, 2001 ABQB 812, 302 AR 1 at para 52. 56 The Rules relating to production and exchange of information have evolved. They now generally call for maximum disclosure and exchange of information in the interest of expeditious, economic, and just resolutions. Requiring defendants to schedule what may potentially be an unnecessary ME is neither timely nor cost-effective. It is beneficial to all parties to avoid the delays and costs associated with unnecessary MEs. As Greckol J. commented in Soodhar v. Bagley, 2003 ABQB 524, 340 AR 178: 57 … It seems to me that rather than heap examination after examination upon the Plaintiff, and expert report upon expert report, clarity and focus in obtaining expert information at the outset, and good faith use of the information already available would better serve the interests of the adversaries and also better serve the overall interests of the litigation process … 57 Requiring plaintiffs to provide their expert reports first has the advantage of allowing defendants to obtain the evidence that will be relied on by the plaintiffs. This provides the defendants with knowledge of the case against them and the evidence that the defendants will face at trial. It allows defendants to focus on what is truly in dispute and to determine whether or not an ME is necessary: Jacobson v. Sveen at para 6. Again, the waiving of the plaintiff's litigation privilege in this context does not result from any action on the part of the defendant, but rather the operation of Rule 5.35. The plaintiff has an onus to advance its own action. 58 The stalemate in this case results from the Plaintiffs' reluctance to move their litigation forward by disclosure of expert reports as required under Rule 5.35. The Plaintiffs' withholding of the medical reports will result in greater delay and expense, a decreased chance of early settlement, and a potential inability of the parties to focus on the real issues. The Plaintiffs would have the Court read into the Rules a requirement as to the timing of the Defendants' initiative, if any, under Rules 5.41 and 5.44. The primary onus is on the Plaintiffs to move the actions forward. Nothing in the Rules prevents the Defendants from waiting for Rule 5.35 disclosure before making a determination with respect to an ME. 2. Consent in Favour of the Physician Conducting the Independent Medical Examination In Veckenstedt v. Youssef, 2011 ABQB 735, 2011 CarswellAlta 2327, 528 A.R. 113, the Plaintiff agreed, at the Defendant's request, to attend an independent medical examination, pursuant to Rule 5.41. The physician nominated to conduct the examination requested the Plaintiff to sign a consent form. The Plaintiff refused on the basis that the Rules of Court do not require him to do so. Master Prowse concluded that the physician's request for the Plaintiff's written consent to conduct the examination was reasonable, and that if the Plaintiff did not provide the written consent, “the consequences of that refusal could be dealt with later by the court” (see paragraph 9). In the course of his Reasons, Master Prowse said, at paragraphs 4-9, and 12-13: 4 Is this a tempest in a teapot? In other words, are the parties failing to fulfil their responsibility under Rule 1.2 (3) to identify the real issues in dispute and facilitate the quickest means of resolving Mr. Veckenstedt's claim at the least expense? Discussion 5 Physicians are trained not to touch their patients without informed consent. Here the physician conducting the IME is a “non-treating physician” who will be touching someone who is not his patient. The physician is understandably concerned to have something in writing confirming that the person being examined consents to that touching. 6 The civil justice system seeks the assistance of the medical profession to accurately evaluate injury claims. If a reasonable request from a member of the medical profession can be accommodated in a way which is not contrary to the Rules of Court, then I think that accommodation should be provided. 7 Honouring the reasonable requests of the IME physician, so long as those requests are not contrary to the Rules of Court, is consistent with the policy reasons espoused by this court in Crone v Blue Cross Life Insurance Co. of Canada, 2001 CarswellAlta 1338, 2001 ABQB 787, 14 C.P.C. (5th) 103, 297 A.R. 351, at paragraph 26, where it stated: First, it seems eminently reasonable that defence medical examiners, indeed all medical professionals, should be left to conduct their medical examinations as they see fit unless there is a compelling reason for the court to interfere or the rules permit it, as for example the rule allowing the presence of a medical nominee chosen by the plaintiff. The court cannot, in any event, compel a doctor to conduct an examination under circumstances which the doctor objects to, so if the courts begin to place constraints on how particular plaintiffs are examined, the predictable effect is that the number of doctors willing to perform defence medical examinations will decline, raising both the price and length of time to complete the discovery process in personal injury actions. 8 In correspondence exchanged between counsel prior to this application, counsel for Mr. Veckenstedt referred to section 14 of the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Alberta Health Professions Act Standards of Practice Consolidation in support of his assertion that a consent form is not required for a Non-Treating Medical Examination (“NTME”). Those provisions state: (4) The physician undertaking the NTME must obtain informed consent from the person for the examination, diagnostic interventions and release of the physician's report. (5) Notwithstanding subsection (4), the physician is not legally required to obtain consent if a person has been ordered by a court order or statutory direction to undergo a NTME; however, the physician is not required to: (a) enforce the terms of a court order or statutory direction, or (b) proceed with an NTME if the person refuses to cooperate with the physician undertaking the NTME [emphasis added] 9 The above quotation, in my view, simply confirms what common sense dictates. If the plaintiff at the time of the examination says to the physician “don't touch me” then that direction would be honoured. The consequences of that refusal could be dealt with later by the court, but nobody would expect the physician to engage in a wrestling match to complete the IME. In my view, it is reasonable that the independent physician would want to confirm ongoing consent on the day of the examination. … 12 When an IME is sought, counsel might agree, under Rule 5.41, that the plaintiff will attend at the examination. In such a case it seems to me appropriate that, when the plaintiff attends for the examination, the plaintiff sign an acknowledgement that he/she continues to consent to the physician touching him/her for the purpose of conducting that examination. 13 Alternatively, the examination might take place under a court order issued pursuant to Rule 5.41(2). The court order should expressly state that the physician is entitled to touch the plaintiff for the purpose of conducting the examination. However, the examination will typically take place weeks or perhaps months after the court order has been issued. It strikes me as reasonable for the physician conducting the IME to obtain an acknowledgement, on the day of the examination, confirming that the plaintiff consents to the physician touching him/her for the purpose of conducting that examination. 3. Does the Rule authorize an order to take DNA? In Branson v. Branson, 2015 ABQB 227, the parties took the view that Rule 5.41 gave the Court authority to order DNA testing. Justice Yamauchi was not so sure. His Lordship said: 18 This Court is not entirely convinced that the Alberta legislature created Rules r 5.41, to allow a court to order an individual to undergo DNA testing. The rule talks about a person's “mental or physical condition.” A person's DNA is not a condition, but a trait. Rules r 5.41 is used in the context of, for example, claims involving personal injury or medical malpractice. 19 This Court is aware of other jurisdictions which have held that DNA testing can be ordered under their rules of civil procedure similar to Rules r 5.41. See e.g. S(DM) v D(J) (1994), 120 D.L.R. (4th) 581 (BCSC); Miller v Staples Estate, 2006 NSCA 140 at paras 30–32, 278 D.L.R. (4th) 535 [Miller]. 20 This Court is of the view that a broad interpretation of Rules r 5.41 might allow it to make such an order. However, it prefers to consider whether it will grant such an order under its inherent jurisdiction which gives it discretion to control its own process to ensure the fairness of a trial, so that all relevant facts be before the court: Stirling v Mangembulude (2000), 272 AR 184 (QB). See also Grayson v Demers, [1975] 2 WWR 289 at paras 21, 24 (Alta SC, App Div), MJR v AR (1994), 28 Alta LR (3d) 224. In all cases, whether the court makes such an order depends on the facts before it. 21 A discretionary order requiring a person to undergo DNA testing is an equitable decision. … 4. Ordering a capacity assessment under the Rule In Melin v. Melin, 2018 ABQB 1056, 2018 CarswellAlta 3186, 81 Alta. L.R. (6th) 194, 86 B.L.R. (5th) 59, 43 E.T.R. (4th) 122, Dale Melin was a 74-year-old man with several health issues. In this litigation he sought to terminate an Enduring Power of Attorney he had given to his son, Brad Melin, and remove Brad as a director of a company started by Dale. Brad cross-applied for “an order directing Dale Melin to attend for a complete geriatric mental assessment to determine his capacity to make determinations with respect to his legal and business affairs.” Though Justice Feehan did not make an order for a capacity assessment, his Lordship held that he had the authority to do so under Rule 5.41 and under legislation. His Lordship said: [109] I conclude this Court does have jurisdiction and authority to order a capacity assessment of Dale Melin, under the circumstances presented in the above fact situation. I conclude that the Adult Guardianship and Trusteeship Act does not “occupy the field” as the only method of a court-ordered capacity assessment. That is clear because s 104 permits a court to order a person to undergo a capacity assessment if that person's capacity to make decisions is in issue “in a proceeding under this Act.” By definition, it does not negate jurisdiction or authority for proceedings other than under the Act. [110] I find that under s 9 of the Powers of Attorney Act, the Court may give its opinion, advice or direction on any matter respecting the management or administration of the donor's property. Determination of capacity of the donor is a matter respecting the management or administration of that donor's property. I also find that r 5.41 of the Alberta Rules of Court provides jurisdiction and authority to the Court to order a capacity assessment, both of its own accord and where a capacity assessment has already been completed through a medical examination of a health care professional of the donor's choice. [111] Section 8 of the Judicature Act is always a residual source of powers the Court may draw upon whenever it is just and equitable to do so, although its use is as a last resort in exceptional circumstances. I also find this Court has authority and jurisdiction pursuant to its parens patriae jurisdiction over vulnerable adults who lack capacity, although that jurisdiction should only be used in exceptional circumstances as an extraordinary step in the clearest of cases where an assessment is necessary. On the question of when such an assessment should be ordered, Justice Feehan said: [112] The real question is not whether this Court has authority and jurisdiction to order a capacity assessment in the present case, but whether it should do so. I accept that a court should be reluctant to order a capacity assessment of an individual who has not put his or her capacity at issue in the litigation, and where it appears that the request for such an assessment is a collateral attack on the matters raised by that person. I accept that the ordering of a capacity assessment in such circumstances should only be a last resort in exceptional circumstances as it seriously impinges upon the individual's autonomy, respect for the individual's decision-making in matters of fundamental personal importance, and should only be used in the clearest of cases in the interests of and to protect the person subject to the order. I accept that the ordering of a capacity assessment is inappropriate to rebut an allegation of incapacity, to merely provide certainty to the Court, or ease concerns of guardians or relatives. Under the circumstances, I do not order a capacity assessment of Dale Melin at the present time. 5. Privilege Rule 217 removes the privilege which once attached to expert medical evidence generated for the purposes of litigation. …Vokes et al. v. Backer (1996), 194 A.R. 343 (Q.B.) at 344, per MacCallum J. 6. A Rule 217 (Previous Rule) Examination Is Not “Independent” In Jacobson v. Sveen, 2000 ABQB 215, 2000 CarswellAlta 291, 262 A.R. 367, Veit J. held that a rule 217 medical examination is not an independent examination, but that all experts have an obligation to give an honest opinion. At pp 372-373, her Ladyship said: …[A] rule 217 examination is not intended to be “independent” in the sense advocated by the plaintiff; the rule 217 examination is intended to be a defence examination. As Allen, J.A., of our Court of Appeal said in Grayson: … whereas the medical practitioner who conducts a medical examination under rule 217 is clearly doing so on behalf of the person seeking the examination, in other words, the person against whom compensation or damages is sought. As our Court of Appeal held in the same case, the examination that is intended to be “independent” is the one that could be ordered by the court under rule 218. … Despite the conclusion that the Defence Medical Examination is not intended to be an “independent” examination of the type proposed by the plaintiff, I re-affirm that, naturally, all experts who provide evidence in legal proceedings must comply with the basic requirement of such witnesses, including an obligation to give an honest opinion. … Expert witnesses in civil cases have several duties and responsibilities when they are in court before a judge, and that includes the duty to give independent and unbiased evidence. They may be advocates for their side and take an adversarial stance, but they cannot mislead the court by giving a less than honest opinion, or one that would compromise their independence and undermine the court's reliance upon them. … … There is likewise a duty under the common law of Alberta for experts to give honest, independent, and unbiased evidence in court. Although the expert's report itself may strongly advance the position of the expert's client, an expert cannot mislead, either in the report or in court. That principle may not be codified in our Rules of Court but is fundamental nonetheless. …[I]f either the party opposite establishes, or the court concludes, that a defence expert is biased, then the court will reject that evidence. Put simply, where an expert assumes the rule sic of an advocate, he or she can no longer be viewed as an expert in the legally correct sense; instead his or her evidence “must be viewed as advocating the care of a party with the attendant diminishment in the credibility”. … 7. The Test for Avoiding the Medical Examination In D. v. Phillips, 2003 ABQB 832, 2003 CarswellAlta 1483, 350 A.R. 24, 27 Alta. L.R. (4th) 251, Clackson J. set out the test to be applied when a plaintiff seeks to avoid a defence medical examination. At pp. 254-255, his Lordship said: In my view the proper test in cases such as these involves balancing the plaintiff's right to be safe and secure against the defendant's right to challenge the plaintiff's assertions. That balance would weigh against the plaintiff where the risk of harm is small and the harm is most likely trifling or transitory. The balance would weigh against the defendants seeking a defence medical where the risk of harm is great and the harm is most likely quite serious. Continuing the analysis, where the risk of harm is great but the harm is likely trivial or transitory then the balance would favor compelling a plaintiff to submit to a defence medical. Where the risk of harm is small but real, and the harm is serious but not especially so, then the interest of the parties are in approximate balance and I think the defence medical should proceed. In that instance however, the court should carefully define the process which will be utilized to obtain the independent assessment. Where the harm is especially serious, then even a small real risk is intolerable and a defence medical would be inappropriate. In Martinez v. Barbeau, 2006 ABQB 363, 2006 CarswellAlta 604, 393 A.R. 365, Burrows J. discussed the meaning Rule 217(4). At pp. 367-368, his Lordship said: Rule 217(4) is reasonably clear as to what it permits the medical practitioner to ask. It is less clear about what it prohibits him from asking. It prohibits an interrogation. It would perhaps be more helpful if it identified the subject matter about which the medical practitioner is not to question the plaintiff. I interpret it as prohibiting questioning about any subject other than the plaintiff's medical condition or medical history. Nothing in the evidence submitted on this application suggests that information about the circumstances of the accident is information about the plaintiff's medical condition or medical history. It may be that information about the circumstances of the accident would be useful to Dr. Lavoie in coming to his opinion. But if he requires that information, he must acquire it from some other source. He should acquire it from defendant's counsel who has examined Mr. Martinez for discovery. Burrows J. then went on to note that Rule 217(4) does not prohibit the physician from putting his or her questions by way of a written questionnaire. At p. 368, his Lordship said: As to the use of a questionnaire to ask for information about the plaintiff's medical condition and medical history, I see no problem. Rule 217(4) does not require that the questions it contemplates be put or answered orally. I see no reason why a questionnaire cannot be used. 8. Stays of Proceedings If the respondent in a R. 217 application made under the previouse Rules was successful in convincing the court that the order sought was outside the rule but the respondent had made use of the same sort of examination in support of his or her claim, some courts denied the application but entered a stay of proceedings until the respondent voluntarily consents to the examination. This was done in Bilinski v. Wangerin (1993), 15 Alta. L.R. (3d) 100 (Q.B.), and in Parenteau v. Courtesy Corner Tourist Service Ltd. (1993), 13 Alta. L.R. (3d) 269 (Q.B.), where Mr. Justice Mason said at pp. 273-74: When a plaintiff in a personal injury case engages a health care specialist to perform examinations and tests upon his or her person to substantiate a claim of physical or other impairment and elects to call such an expert at trial, fairness dictates that as part of his or her trial preparation the defendant be permitted to conduct similar examinations and tests by an expert in the same health care discipline. For these reasons, based on the inherent authority of this Court to ensure fairness in these proceedings, I order that unless the Plaintiff submits to the requested examination by the Defendant's expert in occupational therapy, these proceedings are stayed. The same approach of staying the plaintiff's action until the plaintiff “voluntarily” submitted to examination by the defendant's “functional capacity assessment expert” was taken by Hembroff J. in Souther (Next Friend of) v. Pitre (1995), 27 Alta. L.R. (3d) 15 (Q.B.). In that case, his Lordship referred to Blackburn v. Kochs Trucking Inc. (1988), 58 Alta. L.R. (2d) 358 (Q.B.), where McDonald J. said at pp. 368-69: If the defendants' material were such as to satisfy the court that the proposed examination on behalf of the defendants by an expert other than a medical practitioner (and other than by an expert whose examination would aid a medical practitioner) would be essential to ensure that at trial there was a fair opportunity to meet the case put forward by the plaintiff, and if the plaintiff had refused to consent to the examination, the court, in the exercise of its inherent power to ensure fairness, could order that the action be stayed until the plaintiff submitted to the proposed examination. In Babyn v. Patel (1998), 217 A.R. 187 (Q.B.), Veit J., at p. 190, concluded that: Although the defendants are not entitled to an independent vocational assessment under the Rules, fairness requires that the plaintiff's action be stayed until he consents to submit to an independent vocational assessment. Babyn v. Patel (1998), 217 A.R. 187 (Q.B.) was followed by Master Laycock in Heighes v. Stoutenburg (1998), 234 A.R. 195 (Master). In Stirling v. Mangembulude (2000), 272 A.R. 184 (Q.B.), Chief Justice Moore held that the Court had inherent jurisdiction to order a party to submit to an examination by someone other than a duly qualified medical practitioner even if that party did not intend to adduce similar evidence. At p. 188, his Lordship said: The court, under its inherent jurisdiction to control its own process to ensure the fairness of the trial, can order a plaintiff to submit to an examination by someone other than a duly qualified medical practitioner. … This has typically occurred where the plaintiff intends to adduce evidence through an expert who falls beyond the scope of Rule 217. Fairness requires that a defendant be able to make full answer and defence by being given the opportunity to challenge the plaintiff's evidence. Counsel for Stirling states that this is the only circumstance where the courts will order a stay of the proceedings—that is, when the plaintiff intends to put into evidence a report of an expert who does not meet the definition of a “duly qualified medical practitioner”. While I agree that the weight of authority tends to favour Stirling's interpretation of the law, there are situations where a court has ordered an examination of a plaintiff to ensure the fairness of the proceedings, despite the fact that the plaintiff did not intend to adduce like evidence. Although the definition of “health care professional” in subr. (11) will permit examinations by more practitioners than before, resort to stays of proceeding may continue to be appropropriate in cases involving practitioners still falling outside the rule. 9. Inferences to Be Drawn from Refusal to Be Examined In R. (M.J.) v. R. (A.) (1994), 28 Alta. L.R. (3d) 224 (Q.B.), a defendant in an action for damages in respect of an alleged sexual assault successfully opposed an application for an order under RR. 217 and 218 compelling blood tests. The blood tests would have helped determine the paternity of a child who was born to the plaintiff allegedly as a result of a sexual assault committed by the defendant. Even though the defendant was not required to submit to the blood tests, Kent J. made the following comment (at p. 228) about a possible adverse inference to be taken by the trial judge: However, the Defendant has refused to take the necessary tests. The parentage of the child of the Plaintiff is clearly a central issue to this action. It seems to me that absent a reasonable excuse, the trial judge ought to draw a strong inference from the Defendant's refusal to be tested. 10. Purpose of Examination In Grayson v. Demers, [1975] 2 W.W.R. 289 (Alta. C.A.), Allen J.A. quoted Jaworski v. Wilkinson (1966), 58 W.W.R. 211 (Man. Q.B.), with approval at pp. 295-96: The purpose of the (physical) examination, surely, is to put the parties on a basis of equality, as nearly as may be, and to make available to the court the fullest appraisal of the injuries complained of, and the consequence of such injury. While the plaintiff may have as many and as frequent examinations as she may decide, being limited only as to how many of her experts may testify at the trial, … the defendant, in the absence of the order requested, has no way of discovering the precision of the foundation upon which the plaintiff and her advisers put before the court their opinion as to the severity of the injuries and their sequellae. Nor, in the absence of inquiry by someone other than the plaintiff's own experts, has the court, upon trial of the cause, the benefit of an examination and appraisal of the plaintiff's claims other than in the terms advanced by the plaintiff's own witnesses … Commonly, the disability otherwise suffered by a defendant disappears when, by agreement, counsel arrange to exchange medical reports, or for medical examinations; indeed the absence of reported cases in this province testifies to the reasonableness of the profession in the situation, something indeed to be encouraged. And when examination is ordered, it is ‘to enable the court to obtain the best possible evidence as to the extent of the injuries of the plaintiff’… 11. Defendant Choosing an Out of Jurisdiction Medical Examiner In Gonzalez v. Klassen (2003), 12 Alta. L.R. (4th) 87 (Q.B.), the plaintiff sued the defendant for damages arising from personal injuries alleged to have been suffered by the plaintiff as a result of a motor vehicle accident. The defendant sought a medical examination under Rule 217, but wanted the examination to be conducted by neurologist practising in Vancouver, British Columbia. The plaintiff objected on the basis that there were neurologists available in Alberta. In ordering the plaintiff to attend in Vancouver for the examination, Veit J. said, at pp. 92-93: In summary on this point, although there are Canadian decisions to the effect that the defendant who wishes to conduct a medical examination of a plaintiff outside the jurisdiction must satisfy the court that resort to such an examination is warranted, I am of the view that the burden should be on the plaintiff to give reasons why such an examination is unreasonable rather than on the defendant to prove that such an examination is reasonable. This view is articulated in Barrett: I am not persuaded that the defendant must prove that there are no qualified, independent and available practitioners in Manitoba before the plaintiff can be ordered to submit to an examination in Ontario. The inconvenience and hardship of travel must be assessed in each case, and must be balanced against the prima facie right of the examining party to choose the physician. Just as a plaintiff does not have to justify his choice of attending or treating physician, so a defendant should not have to justify her choice of examining physician. It may well be that a plaintiff's refusal to attend for a medical examination outside the province would be justified if, within Alberta, there were no conflicts with physicians and there were a wide range of qualified physicians from which the defendant could choose. Each refusal must be examined on its own circumstances. 12. Charter Considerations Charter challenges to specific rules of court require the court to consider not only the rule challenged but also the scheme within which the rule operates: The Defendant challenges the application on the basis of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Because of the reasons above, it is not necessary to decide that issue. However, it is appropriate to make some comment. As I said above, our Rules of Court are designed to ensure that litigation is conducted in a fair manner. Striking down a rule or a portion thereof may have the unintended effect of upsetting that balance of fairness for all cases. Using R. 217 again as an example, if it is found that the ability to order a medical examination which included the taking of blood or other invasive procedures was contrary to either s. 7 or s. 8 of the Charter, then defendants would be deprived of their ability to fully defend themselves against a claim based upon the plaintiff's physical condition. At this stage of medical knowledge, a physical examination without testing is not a real medical examination. The same reasoning may apply to an order made under R. 218. Counsel for the Attorney-General argues that in a challenge based upon s. 7, s. 8 or s. 13 (the sections involved here), the Court must look at the claim in context of the legislative scheme involved. Indeed, that is the view of Mr. Justice Cory in the Supreme Court of Canada in R. v. Wholesale Travel Group Inc. (1991), 67 C.C.C. (3d) 193. He says at p. 243: It is now clear that the Charter is to be interpreted in light of the context in which the claim arises. Context is relevant both with respect to the delineation of the meaning and scope of Charter rights, as well as to the determination of the balance to be struck between individual rights and the interests of society. In the case of the Rules of Court, the balance that needs to be examined is the need to be fair as between litigants against the effect that any rule has upon the individual in question. In my view, for example, R. 217 does not offend the Charter because the person who would be objecting to the giving of blood is the very person who has put that matter in issue before the court. An order under R. 218 is more problematic where the person involved does not consent. Each case obviously depends upon its facts. But the portion of the rule that allows for a medical examination including testing is not in all circumstances contrary to the Charter. R. (M.J.) v. R. (A.) (1994), 28 Alta. L.R. (3d) 224 (Q.B.), at 228-29, per Kent J.

Timing of the exchange of reports In Erketu v.
Wilson, 2013 ABQB 247, 2013 CarswellAlta 534, 560 A.R.
L.R.

(5th) 35, Justice Nielsen considered this issue: “whether the Court should order that a defendant in a personal injury action make its position known on an ME under Rule 5.41 prior to the plaintiff disclosing its expert report(s) under Rule 5.35.” In holding that a defendant should not be so ordered, his Lordship said, at paragraphs 32–58: 32 There is no dispute that the expert reports sought by the Defendants are covered by litigation privilege.
Litigation privilege attaches to documents that have been created for the dominant purpose of furthering litigation: Opron Construction Co v.
Alberta (1989), 100 AR 58, 1989 ABCA 279 (Canlii).

The purpose of litigation privilege is to create a zone of privacy in relation to pending or apprehended litigation by providing a protected area to facilitate investigation and preparation of a case for trial by the adversarial advocate: Blank v.
Canada (Minister of Justice), 2006 SCC 39, [2006] 2 SCR 319 at para 34.
The rationale for the privilege is that the adversarial system requires that each party be able to prepare its case in private: Pinder v.
Sproule, 2003 ABQB 33, 333 AR 132 at para 48.
33 An expert report prepared in contemplation of litigation is clearly subject to litigation privilege, and the party who ordered the report is entitled to suppress its disclosure.

Litigation privilege can be waived expressly or by knowingly providing a copy of the document to another party, or by attempting to rely on the privileged documents to obtain some relief from the Court: Pinder v.
Sproule at para 10.
Litigation privilege is waived when expert reports are used in Court.
34 Rule 5.35 is a statutory exception to litigation privilege.
Unlike Former Rule 218.1, Rule 5.35 provides a sequential exchange of expert reports.
It generally dictates that the party bearing the primary onus of proof must waive litigation privilege with respect to the expert report(s) upon which that party intends to rely.
In a personal injury action, this results in a plaintiff waiving litigation privilege with respect to the expert report(s) it intends to adduce at trial.

35 Rule 5.44(3), like Former Rule 217(7), is another statutory exception to litigation privilege, relating specifically to medical-legal reports and reports of medical examinations sought by a defendant after an ME under Rule 5.41: Andre v.
Wiebe, 2000 ABQB 946, 284 AR 378 at para 7.
It does not result only in disclosure of the report(s) the plaintiff intends to adduce at trial, but, rather, disclosure of reports of every medical examination previously or subsequently made.
36 In my view, the question is not whether Rule 5.44(3) impinges on litigation privilege.
Clearly, it does do so.
If a defendant does not request an ME thereby triggering Rule 5.44(3), litigation privilege remains on any expert report which a plaintiff does not intend to adduce.
37 However, a plaintiff, in order to advance the action, must waive privilege on expert reports upon which it intends to rely, under Rule 5.35.
38 The Plaintiffs argue that the Rules contain a “gap” and the Court should require the Defendants to make a decision on an ME prior to the Plaintiffs disclosing under Rule 5.35.
39 In my view, there is no gap in the Rules.
The Plaintiffs argue that the use of Rule 5.35 to obtain the Plaintiffs' medical expert reports without first conducting an ME would render Rule 5.44(3) useless.
I do not agree.
The two Rules can work in conjunction to provide the Court with the most complete evidence of a plaintiff's medical condition when that is at issue in litigation.
40 The onus is on a plaintiff to advance its action.
Rule 5.35 generally reflects this onus in requiring the party with the onus to disclose first.

41 The real question is whether there is anything in the Rules which prevents a defendant from waiting to rely on Rules 5.41 and 5.44 until after a plaintiff has disclosed its expert report(s) under Rule 5.35.
42 In fact, there is nothing in the Rules that prevents a defendant from doing so.
Nothing in the Rules dictates that steps pursuant to Rules 5.41 and 5.44 must occur before the plaintiff discloses pursuant to Rule 5.35.

Although Rule 1.2(3) now mandates that all parties must facilitate the quickest means of resolving the claim at the least expense, nothing in the Rules requires a defendant to take any initiative under Rule 5.41 prior to the plaintiff's disclosure under Rule 5.35.
It would have been a simple thing for the legislature to provide otherwise.

43 Rules 5.41(1) and 5.44(3), and Former Rule 217, have existed in relatively the same form since the 1968 Rules of Court as a mechanism for the defendant to have physical access to a plaintiff and to have disclosure of records of the plaintiff's previous medical examinations prior to trial.
As explained by MacDonald J. in Petersen v.
Shepard (1985), 58 AR 240, [1985] AJ No 651 at para 7 (QB), this was important because previously there was no rule which required the disclosure of expert reports prior to trial.
If no ME was performed under Former Rule 217, a defendant could learn of an expert's evidence for the first time only at the actual trial.
This procedure of keeping evidence hidden from the other party until trial was a system of “trial by ambush”.
44 This system of “trial by ambush” was altered in 1985 when Rule 5.35, in its original form of Former Rule 218.1, was introduced.
Former Rule 218.1(1) became another limit on “trial by ambush” since it abolished the litigation privilege on expert reports by requiring disclosure prior to trial.
The adoption of Former Rule 218.1 did not result in the abolition of Former Rule 217.
45 Rule 5.35 and Rules 5.41 to 5.44 serve different purposes.
Rule 5.35 requires the disclosure of expert reports that will be relied on at trial.
This allows a defendant to know the evidence the plaintiff will be relying on and provides an opportunity to counter the expert evidence.
Rule 5.35 relates to the disclosure of any type of expert evidence in any type of litigation.
46 Rules 5.41 to 5.44 only relate to the medical evidence of a litigant's condition.

Allowing a physical examination of a plaintiff and the disclosure of reports of previous medical examinations ensures that the court will have adequate evidence to assess a plaintiff's claim when it relates to a medical condition.
The disclosure of reports of previous medical examinations allows a defendant to assess issues surrounding the cause, nature, or aggravation of the injuries.
The unique nature of a claim for medical injuries requires unique rules.

A party who has put his or her physical condition in issue should not be in a position to deny the opposite party the right to ascertain his or her physical condition by suitable examination by a medical practitioner: Jacobson v.
Sveen, 2000 ABQB 215, 262 AR 367 at paras 42 and 43.
Rule 5.44(3) is an additional type of disclosure of records and an additional exchange of expert reports.
This provision has specific application only when an ME is conducted.
Otherwise, Rule 5.35 governs the exchange of expert reports.
47 The Plaintiffs are concerned that if they are required to disclose their expert reports, the examiner who performs an ME may be biased by the information.
Lefsrud J. came to this conclusion in Soodhar v.
With respect, I reject this as supporting the withholding of the expert reports required to be disclosed under Rule 5.35.
48 An ME is a defendant's examination, not an independent examination.
As stated by the Alberta Court of Appeal in Grayson v.

Demers, [1975] 2 WWR 289, [1974] AJ No 291 (CA), “the medical practitioner who conducts an ME under rule 217 is clearly doing so on behalf of the person seeking the examination, in other words, the person against whom compensation or damages is sought”.
49 A medical professional performing an ME has an obligation to be objective and to provide an honest opinion.
Seeing another expert's report does not, in and of itself, undermine an expert's opinion: Jacobson v.
Sveen at paras 36 and 44.

Further, potential bias created by the medical professional having access to the plaintiffs' medical reports prior to the ME can be assessed under cross-examination and determined by a trial judge: Rosario-Paquet v.
Hudec, 2000 ABQB 762, 279 AR 319 at para 24.
Trial judges are accustomed to assessing reliability and credibility and attributing appropriate weight to evidence.
They are accustomed to assessing competing expert evidence.
As a result, the potential for bias, without more, does not support the withholding of the Plaintiffs' expert reports until after the Defendants have moved under Rule 5.44(3).

50 I note in this regard that the Plaintiffs concede that subsequent MEs could be ordered by the Defendants after disclosure is triggered following the first ME, a position which is consistent with Veit J.'s decision in Jacobson v.
Sveen.
Any potential for bias would exist with respect to those subsequent MEs.
51 This approach is consistent with Rule 1.2.

In particular, the Rules should be interpreted to facilitate the quickest means of resolving a claim at the least expense, and to oblige the parties to communicate honestly, openly and in a timely way.

52 This approach is also consistent with the purposes stated in Rule 5.1, in particular encouraging early disclosure of facts and records, facilitating evaluation of the parties' positions, and discouraging conduct that unnecessarily or improperly delays proceedings or unnecessarily increases the cost of them.

53 To rule otherwise would be to require defendants in such actions to potentially incur unnecessary costs to obtain the very disclosure to which they are entitled under Rule 5.35 and which they will receive in any event prior to the matter being set down for trial.
54 Unlike the Former Rules, the Rules no longer provide specific instructions regarding the timing of the exchange of expert reports.
The only requirement is that the party bearing the onus of proof provide its reports first.
This is a change from the specific deadlines set out in the Former Rules.
The Rules allow the parties to determine their own timelines for the litigation process and the disclosure of expert reports.
55 Although the timelines from Former Rule 218.1 are not contained in Rule 5.35, the purpose of Rule 5.35 remains the same.
It is designed to prevent one party from surprising the other with expert testimony.
The emphasis is on a fair and workable process for disclosure: Stewart Estate v.
TAQA North Ltd., 2012 ABQB 87, [2012] AJ No 188 at para 19.

It requires parties to give notice of their expert evidence and to waive litigation privilege in time to allow the other side to know the case he or she has to meet and to allow a reasonable chance to respond.
As stated by Slatter J., as he then was, “It allows the experts to focus on what is truly in dispute.
The rule was never intended to be a chess game between counsel”: Wade v.
Baxter, 2001 ABQB 812, 302 AR 1 at para 52.
56 The Rules relating to production and exchange of information have evolved.
They now generally call for maximum disclosure and exchange of information in the interest of expeditious, economic, and just resolutions.
Requiring defendants to schedule what may potentially be an unnecessary ME is neither timely nor cost-effective.
It is beneficial to all parties to avoid the delays and costs associated with unnecessary MEs.
As Greckol J. commented in Soodhar v.

Bagley, 2003 ABQB 524, 340 AR 178: 57 … It seems to me that rather than heap examination after examination upon the Plaintiff, and expert report upon expert report, clarity and focus in obtaining expert information at the outset, and good faith use of the information already available would better serve the interests of the adversaries and also better serve the overall interests of the litigation process … 57 Requiring plaintiffs to provide their expert reports first has the advantage of allowing defendants to obtain the evidence that will be relied on by the plaintiffs.
This provides the defendants with knowledge of the case against them and the evidence that the defendants will face at trial.
It allows defendants to focus on what is truly in dispute and to determine whether or not an ME is necessary: Jacobson v.
Sveen at para 6.
Again, the waiving of the plaintiff's litigation privilege in this context does not result from any action on the part of the defendant, but rather the operation of Rule 5.35.
The plaintiff has an onus to advance its own action.
58 The stalemate in this case results from the Plaintiffs' reluctance to move their litigation forward by disclosure of expert reports as required under Rule 5.35.

The Plaintiffs' withholding of the medical reports will result in greater delay and expense, a decreased chance of early settlement, and a potential inability of the parties to focus on the real issues.
The Plaintiffs would have the Court read into the Rules a requirement as to the timing of the Defendants' initiative, if any, under Rules 5.41 and 5.44.
The primary onus is on the Plaintiffs to move the actions forward.
Nothing in the Rules prevents the Defendants from waiting for Rule 5.35 disclosure before making a determination with respect to an ME.

Ordering a capacity assessment under the Rule In Melin v.
Melin, 2018 ABQB 1056, 2018 CarswellAlta 3186, 81 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 122, Dale Melin was a 74-year-old man with several health issues.
In this litigation he sought to terminate an Enduring Power of Attorney he had given to his son, Brad Melin, and remove Brad as a director of a company started by Dale.

Brad cross-applied for “an order directing Dale Melin to attend for a complete geriatric mental assessment to determine his capacity to make determinations with respect to his legal and business affairs.” Though Justice Feehan did not make an order for a capacity assessment, his Lordship held that he had the authority to do so under Rule 5.41 and under legislation.
His Lordship said: [109] I conclude this Court does have jurisdiction and authority to order a capacity assessment of Dale Melin, under the circumstances presented in the above fact situation.
I conclude that the Adult Guardianship and Trusteeship Act does not “occupy the field” as the only method of a court-ordered capacity assessment.

That is clear because s 104 permits a court to order a person to undergo a capacity assessment if that person's capacity to make decisions is in issue “in a proceeding under this Act.” By definition, it does not negate jurisdiction or authority for proceedings other than under the Act.
[110] I find that under s 9 of the Powers of Attorney Act, the Court may give its opinion, advice or direction on any matter respecting the management or administration of the donor's property.
Determination of capacity of the donor is a matter respecting the management or administration of that donor's property.

I also find that r 5.41 of the Alberta Rules of Court provides jurisdiction and authority to the Court to order a capacity assessment, both of its own accord and where a capacity assessment has already been completed through a medical examination of a health care professional of the donor's choice.

[111] Section 8 of the Judicature Act is always a residual source of powers the Court may draw upon whenever it is just and equitable to do so, although its use is as a last resort in exceptional circumstances.

I also find this Court has authority and jurisdiction pursuant to its parens patriae jurisdiction over vulnerable adults who lack capacity, although that jurisdiction should only be used in exceptional circumstances as an extraordinary step in the clearest of cases where an assessment is necessary.

On the question of when such an assessment should be ordered, Justice Feehan said: [112] The real question is not whether this Court has authority and jurisdiction to order a capacity assessment in the present case, but whether it should do so.

I accept that a court should be reluctant to order a capacity assessment of an individual who has not put his or her capacity at issue in the litigation, and where it appears that the request for such an assessment is a collateral attack on the matters raised by that person.

I accept that the ordering of a capacity assessment in such circumstances should only be a last resort in exceptional circumstances as it seriously impinges upon the individual's autonomy, respect for the individual's decision-making in matters of fundamental personal importance, and should only be used in the clearest of cases in the interests of and to protect the person subject to the order.
I accept that the ordering of a capacity assessment is inappropriate to rebut an allegation of incapacity, to merely provide certainty to the Court, or ease concerns of guardians or relatives.
Under the circumstances, I do not order a capacity assessment of Dale Melin at the present time.

They may be advocates for their side and take an adversarial stance, but they cannot mislead the court by giving a less than honest opinion, or one that would compromise their independence and undermine the court's reliance upon them. … … There is likewise a duty under the common law of Alberta for experts to give honest, independent, and unbiased evidence in court.
Although the expert's report itself may strongly advance the position of the expert's client, an expert cannot mislead, either in the report or in court.

That principle may not be codified in our Rules of Court but is fundamental nonetheless. …[I]f either the party opposite establishes, or the court concludes, that a defence expert is biased, then the court will reject that evidence.

Put simply, where an expert assumes the rule sic of an advocate, he or she can no longer be viewed as an expert in the legally correct sense; instead his or her evidence “must be viewed as advocating the care of a party with the attendant diminishment in the credibility”. … 7.

paragraphs.text: (1) Unless otherwise ordered by the Court, a person who is to be the subject of a medical examination by a health care professional may elect to do one or more of the following: (a) nominate a health care professional to be present during the medical examination; (b) videotape the medical examination; (c) make a word-for-word recording of the medical examination. (2) The Court may (a) define or limit the presence or role of the nominated health care professional, (b) direct that any part of the medical examination, including any standardized tests, not be recorded, and (c) otherwise provide direction as to the conduct of the medical examination.
