paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.42:1 Rule 5.42 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.42. 1. Dispensing with Recording of Examination In Nguyen v. Koehn, 2012 ABQB 655, 2012 CarswellAlta 1849, 550 A.R. 272, 77 Alta. L.R. (5th) 418, the plaintiff sued the defendant as a result of injuries suffered in a motor vehicle accident. The plaintiff wanted the defence medical examination of the plaintiff to be videotaped. The defendant did not want to retain the services of any of the orthopaedic specialists who were prepared to have the examination videotaped. A Master dismissed the defendant's application for an order dispensing with the videotaping of the examination. On appeal to a Justice of the Court of Queen's Bench, Madam Justice Moreau said, at paragraph 46: 46 In all of the circumstances, a fair result that would give effect to the purpose of Rule 5.42 would be to allow the Appellant, at his option to be exercised within 30 days of the release of these reasons, to select a health care professional who will permit videotaping, or instead to select one who will accept only the presence of a nominee. If the Appellant decides on the latter option, he will be responsible for the payment of any costs associated with the attendance of the nominee to be selected by the Respondent which are over and above those that would be entailed with videotaping the examination. In the course of her ruling, Madam Justice Moreau said, at paragraphs 35–38, 41-42, and 44-45: 35 Clearly, this is not the situation under new Alberta Rule 5.42(1). Unlike the state of the law in Ontario, Rule 5.42(1) contains no requirement that a plaintiff demonstrate the potential for a bona fide concern as to the reliability of the doctor's account of any statements made by the plaintiff during the examination. I am of the view that it is for the party seeking to dispense with videotaping to justify the court exercising its discretion to deprive the person being examined of his or her entitlement to have the examination videotaped under the new Rule. 36 The Appellant submits that without a waiver of videotaping in this case, the equal playing field created by permitting defence medical examinations will be disrupted, particularly given there is no requirement that a medical examination of the plaintiff performed at his or her behest be videotaped. While Nistor[Nistor v. Kankolongo (2007), 431 A.R. 367 (Alta. Q.B.)] was decided under the old Rules when the right to have a nominee present at a defence medical examination was considered absolute, the comments of Bielby J (as she then was) at para 23 of that case regarding the difference between the two types of medical examinations nonetheless are germane: No one suggests that the Legislature created the right to have a nominee present other than as a means of ensuring accuracy and fair play during an examination ordered and paid for by a party opposite in interest. Different considerations apply when a party is being examined by his own physician.”[Emphasis added.] 37 Doherty JA, who concurred in the result in Bellamy[Bellamy v. Johnson (1992) 90 D.L.R. (4th) 564 (Ont. C.A.)], expanded at para 28 on the different considerations that apply when a plaintiff is being examined by a doctor of the defendant's choosing rather his or her own physician: It is unrealistic to view the relationship between the examining doctor and the plaintiff-examinee as akin to that of the relationship which exists when a patient goes to a doctor seeking treatment or advice. It is equally unrealistic to expect that the same rapport based on mutual trust and confidentiality should be expected or even sought. When determining whether the tape recording of the examination would interfere with an effective medical evaluation, the realities of the relationship between the doctor and the plaintiff-examinee must be borne in mind. It is not enough that the presence of the device could inhibit the development of the trust and confidence which would be expected in a normal doctor-patient relationship. Those features are not part of the “defence medical” dynamic. 38 Moreover, as noted by Bielby J in Nistor at para 24, if the legislature had intended that defendants retain an unfettered right to challenge a plaintiff's case, it would not have introduced the Rules relating to nominees. The same point can be made in relation to videotaping. … 41 There is no evidence indicating why the six orthopaedic specialists have refused videotaping and no evidence that it might impair their ability to conduct a proper and effective medical examination. It is the refusal of those orthopaedic specialists to permit videotaping that is limiting the Appellant's choices, not the actions of the Respondent in insisting on an option the legislature has determined he may elect to exercise. 42 The Appellant argued that plaintiffs could use Rule 5.42(1) to artificially narrow the pool of available health care practitioners by asking for videotaping in every case. I am not satisfied that asking for videotaping, which clearly is an option for a plaintiff under the new Rules, is indicative of a mischievous purpose. In the appropriate case, where there are cogent reasons provided to justify dispensing with videotaping, the Court has the discretion under Rule 5.42(1) and (2) to do so, but not without considering various alternatives. … 44 In this particular case, the pool of available Edmonton orthopaedic specialists willing to allow videotaping of the defence medical examination is limited to a minimum of four and a potential maximum of eight (if one includes the four who were contacted on behalf of the Appellant but who have not yet responded). I note that counsel for the Appellant did not provide specific reasons why he does not wish to select any of the specialists from that pool. I also note that counsel for the Appellant does not wish to retain medical professionals in related specialties to conduct the defence medical examination. At least one of those medical professionals (Dr. Hoffmann) is prepared to have his examination videotaped. 45 The evidence also discloses that Dr. Guy Lavoie signed a form addressed to him by counsel for the Appellant indicating that while he would not permit his medical examination to be videotaped, he would permit a nominee to be present. Counsel for the Appellant named Dr. Guy Lavoie as one of the three orthopaedic specialists he favoured to perform the examination. 2. Is There A Right To Videotape a Minor Injury Regulation Certified Medical Examination? In Gordon v. Taylor, 2014 ABQB 11, 2014 CarswellAlta 18, 579 A.R. 387, 53 C.P.C. (7th) 396, Madam Justice Ross said, at paragraph 38: 38 I conclude that the entitlement to videotaping under the Rules does not apply to CMEs under the MIR. The purpose of the Rules provision, to provide protection to the examinee due to the perceived partiality of medical examinations under the Rules, has no application due to the neutral appointment process under the MIR. Further, the neutral appointment process under the MIR and access to CMEs would be put in jeopardy by providing an entitlement to videotape CMEs, which could defeat rather than promote the objective of the MIR. Justice Ross also doubted that the Court had inherent jurisdiction to order the videotaping of certified medical examination. At paragraphs 41-42, her Ladyship said: 41 However, I add that I am not satisfied that the Court's inherent jurisdiction as described in Bellamy applies to CMEs. Bellamy and related case law has dealt with videotaping of medical examinations performed pursuant to court procedural rules. In Bellamy, Brooke JA, for the majority, and Doherty JA, concurring, both based their conclusions on the court's inherent jurisdiction to control the discovery process: Bellamy at paras 8-9 and 15–26. CMEs are not a part of the discovery process. 42 In my view the proper approach is again that set out in Benc. The Court may supplement MIR procedure only “in a fashion consistent with the object and spirit of the [MIR]”: Benc, at para 1. I have already concluded an entitlement to videotape is not consistent with the objective of the MIR. A discretionary order to videotape based on the current policy under the new Rules would be equally inconsistent with the objective of the MIR. I do not need to decide whether there may exist special circumstances in which a discretionary order to videotape would promote the objective of the MIR, as none are presented in this case. 3. Nominee Taking Notes In Gutierrez v. Jeske, 2004 ABQB 105, 2004 CarswellAlta 202, 355 A.R. 62, Moen J. concluded that a medical practitioner nominated under Rule 217(5) to be present is permitted to take notes during the examination. At p. 66, her Ladyship said: Rule 217(5) does not address the issue of whether or not a nominee doctor can take notes. However, taking notes is distinguishable from either videotaping or tape recording the examination. If the nominee is to fulfill his or her function in ensuring that the examination is accurately recorded, a nominee must be able to take notes. Note taking does not have the same impact on trial fairness, since its use in trial would be to refresh the nominee's memory, not as evidence as a videotape or tape recording. It seems to me that if a nominee is there to protect the interests of the Plaintiff, then that nominee would be unnecessarily constrained by not being able to take notes. I want to make it clear that the notes to be taken are notes taken by the nominee doctor and not by a third party accompanying the doctor. That would be disruptive. If the note taking or any other behaviour on the part of the nominee doctor is distracting to the independent medical examiner, then there are a number of courses open to the independent medical examiner and to the Defendants. Those courses of action may include, speaking privately to the doctor about the behaviour that is of concern, terminating the independent medical examination, or continuing the independent medical examination and writing the observations of the nominee's behaviour in the expert report.

paragraphs.text: (1) Unless the Court otherwise orders, the party who applies for the order for a medical examination must pay the cost of the medical examination. (2) Unless the Court otherwise orders, the cost of (a) the attendance of a nominated health care professional at a medical examination, or (b) videotaping or recording a medical examination, is to be paid by the party appointing the nominated health care professional or electing to have the medical examination videotaped or recorded. (3) The party arranging for the videotaping or recording must provide a copy of the videotape or recording to the other party as soon as practicable after the medical examination is completed. (4) The videotape or recording (a) may be shown or played at trial only with the Court's permission, and (b) may only be used to verify events at the medical examination.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.43:1 Rule 5.43 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.43. Who Must Pay for Examination I agree, of course, with the defendant's assertion that the general rule is that a litigant must pay for their own case; that position is well established in the case law. However, that general rule has no application to independent medical examinations. Those examinations are requested by the party opposite; parties opposite are not entitled to such an examination; if the court allows the party opposite to have such an unusual examination, it is entitled to put terms and conditions on the holding of an independent medical examination. An independent medical examination is not held to advance the plaintiff's case; it is held to advance the case of the party opposite. Rule 217(2) must therefore mean that it must then be up to the party opposite to pay all of the expenses of that examination: the cost of the physician who holds the examination, the cost of getting the plaintiff to the examination, the cost of having a nominee of the plaintiff at the examination, etc. If Rule 217(2) had intended the obligation of the party opposite to pay for the examination to be restricted in any way, it would have said so. Instead, the language of Rule 217(2) is as broad as possible. Rule 217(4) states that the physician conducting the independent medical examination may ask the person being examined questions relating to their medical condition and medical history, but may not “interrogate” the person being examined. Where, as in this case, the examination is to be a psychiatric one, it will obviously be necessary for the defendant's physician to ask the plaintiff many questions; this clinical examination is the primary way in which the physician will be able to acquire information about the plaintiff's psychiatric condition. It is particularly important in this type of examination for a plaintiff to be assured, through the attendance of a physician of her choice, that the examination will be properly conducted and accurately reported. The attendance of the plaintiff's nominee physician is therefore an integral step in the independent medical examination process. . . . . . Where a party opposite wishes to have an independent medical examination, it must pay for all of the the costs associated with such an examination. For example, it must pay the cost of the physician who will conduct the examination, of any nurse or other assistant who may be required, travel expenses for the party to be examined to attend the examination, the cost of equipment and tools used during the examination, the cost of the interpreter required to conduct the examination, etc. Importantly, in the context of this application, the party must pay for the costs of the medical nominee of the party to be examined to attend the examination. Morales v. Seymour (1997), 52 Alta. L.R. (3d) 112 (Q.B.), at pp. 117-18, per Veit J. Mr. Justice Lee would restrict Morales v. Seymour (1997), 52 Alta. L.R. (3d) 112 (Q.B.) to its own facts. In Garrido v. Pui (1998), 64 Alta. L.R. (3d) 14 (Q.B.), at p. 17, he said: I believe that the decision in Morales v. Seymour, supra should be restricted to the unique fact situation that was before the Court. In Pohynayko v. Vries, 2001 ABCA 20, 2001 CarswellAlta 68, 277 A.R. 72, 94 Alta. L.R. (3d) 288, Rooke J. (ad hoc), at pp. 77-78, agreed that Morales v. Seymour (1997), 52 Alta. L.R. (3d) 112 (Q.B.) should be restricted to its unique facts. The learned chambers justice noted that in Morales the plaintiff claimed impecuniosity and the cost of the attendance of the plaintiff's medical practitioner might be “quite high”. He further noted that the plaintiff was Spanish speaking and needed an interpreter. Finally, Lee J. seemed to accept the plaintiff's description of the role of the plaintiff medical practitioner in Morales, at p. 116: Not only will her psychiatrist protect her interests during the examination, and give her information as may be required during the course of the examination, but that physician will also be a witness, if necessary to what happened during the examination. Lee J. then noted that in the application before him the plaintiff was not impecunious, the matter was a “relatively uncomplicated medical matter” (as opposed to the psychiatric issues involved in Morales), the medical practitioner was to have no special role in the examination, and the plaintiff had no language difficulties. He then said at pp. 17-18: Based on these factual differences, there is a distinction therefore in the role of the medical nominee of the Plaintiff herein, and a question as to what purpose the medical nominee served. There is no doubt that according to the Rule, the Plaintiff has a right to have a medical nominee attend at an independent medical examination requested by the Defendant. However it seems that there should be some evidence as to the purpose or benefit gained by that attendance in order to saddle the Defendant with the costs of the medical nominee's presence. . . . . . Even with respect to the Rule itself, it is silent as to who should bear the costs for the medical nominee. Clearly, if Rule 217(5) had intended that the Defendant pay for the Plaintiff's medical nominee, the Rule could have so stated. While the opposite conclusion is equally arguable, the non-specificity of the Rule in question here as to payment for the Plaintiff's medical nominee implies some sort of discretion, to be exercised judicially based on a concept such as “reasonableness”. For example, the necessity, contribution of, or requirement for the Plaintiff's medical nominee would reasonably require compensation for the Plaintiff's medical nominee to be paid for by the Defendant. The opposite result would occur in circumstances similar to the facts before me. Generally, a litigant must pay for the cost of their [sic] own case. While the Defendant is the party that requested the independent medical examination, and while the Plaintiff was entitled to have a nominee present during this independent medical examination, that does not necessarily mean that the Defendant must be responsible for the costs of the medial nominee. There are many cases where legislation give [sic] parties rights but where the party exercising the benefit of that right invariably pays for the costs of exercising that right. In Pohynayko v. Vries, 2001 ABCA 20, 2001 CarswellAlta 68, 277 A.R. 72, 94 Alta. L.R. (3d) 288, Rooke J. (ad hoc), speaking for the court, held that the costs associated with the nomination under Rule 217(5) of a medical practitioner to be present during the examination must be first borne by the party nominating the medical practitioner. That party, if successful in the litigation then can seek to recover those costs. At pp. 74-75, Rooke J. said: That rule 217(5) is a permissive right is unchallenged. That is, it is the right of a party being examined by a medical practitioner to nominate another medical practitioner to attend the examination, without providing any other justification. However, it is not a compulsory requirement. The nomination of such a medical practitioner is not caused by an independent medical examination request by the defendant, but rather follows from it, as a discretionary right that may be exercised by the person to be examined, if so desired. However, as to the costs of the nominee's attendance, it is, in substance, no different from other costs (mandatory or discretionary) that a plaintiff will incur in prosecuting an action. In each case, as with other pretrial steps, the plaintiff would be required to pay the costs associated with such examinations and steps in the first instance. A successful plaintiff can then apply for reimbursement of these costs at the end of the proceeding. The same rules, in the normal case apply to the costs incurred by the plaintiff relating to the attendance of a nominee for a rule 217 examination. It is to be noted that rule 217(2) provides that the “examination” is to be at the expense of the party seeking it. It was conceded before us, and I concur, that that includes all of the costs necessary for the examination—obtaining the independent medical examiner, the reasonable transportation costs for the attendance of the party to be examined, and any ancillary tests that are done at the request of the defendant. However, in my view, the attendance of the nominee is not necessary for the examination, but rather, as noted, is merely a discretionary right that the plaintiff may exercise. 2. Use of the video recording In Kohlendorfer v. Northcott, 2013 ABQB 145, 2013 CarswellAlta 384, 558 A.R. 227, Justice Read discussed the use of video recordings of independent medical examinations. Her Ladyship set out the facts before as follows: The plaintiffs in two separate actions had videotaped, at their request, medical examinations they underwent by medical experts chosen by the defendants. The plaintiffs provided the videotapes of the examinations to counsel for the defendants but with restrictions as to their use. Notably, the plaintiffs sought to disable the defendants from permitting the examining experts to review the videotapes before finalizing their experts' reports. At paragraphs 23, and 38–40, Justice Read said: 23 Having considered these Foundational Rules, I have concluded that they suggest an interpretation of R. 5.43 which permits the defendant's expert to review the video recording before completing his or her report and which permits, as well, defendant's counsel to review the recording. … 38 In conclusion, the defendants in both these actions seek to permit the examiner who completed the DME to review the video recording of that DME before completing their report. There is no valid reason for disabling them from doing so and many reasons to permit it. There is also no valid reason to disable defence counsel from reviewing such video recordings and many good reasons to permit it, as outlined above. Any other defence examiner whose examination is videotaped in these actions, should be permitted the same opportunity to review the video recordings of their examinations before completing their reports. 39 Medical professionals are well used to treating information confidentially and are bound by their professional rules from misusing it. Legal counsel are also bound by their professional rules and by the general rule that information obtained in the course of litigation may be used only for the purposes of that litigation. I do agree with the plaintiffs, however, that some limits are appropriate for video recordings. They are, or may be, sensitive in nature, and unlike other information which may potentially be used in court, the New Rules do not require that they be filed or otherwise made public. Generally, there will be no reason to permit or require the defendant personally to view these recordings. Often, as well, in personal injury claims, the defendant's insurers will also be involved. As a general rule, there seems to be no reason to permit an insurance adjuster to view the recordings. While the defendant Setiono requests permission for the insurers involved to view the recordings, counsel for that defendant have not explained why it is necessary or helpful in this proceeding to permit this. I do not foreclose the possibility such disclosure will be necessary in another case but here, I will disable them from doing so. 40 As well, no one sought the ability to permit any other of the defendants' experts to view the video recordings made during the examination of another of the defendant's experts so I will leave that question to another day.

Who Must Pay for Examination I agree, of course, with the defendant's assertion that the general rule is that a litigant must pay for their own case; that position is well established in the case law.
However, that general rule has no application to independent medical examinations.

Those examinations are requested by the party opposite; parties opposite are not entitled to such an examination; if the court allows the party opposite to have such an unusual examination, it is entitled to put terms and conditions on the holding of an independent medical examination.
An independent medical examination is not held to advance the plaintiff's case; it is held to advance the case of the party opposite.

Rule 217(2) must therefore mean that it must then be up to the party opposite to pay all of the expenses of that examination: the cost of the physician who holds the examination, the cost of getting the plaintiff to the examination, the cost of having a nominee of the plaintiff at the examination, etc.
If Rule 217(2) had intended the obligation of the party opposite to pay for the examination to be restricted in any way, it would have said so.
Instead, the language of Rule 217(2) is as broad as possible.

Rule 217(4) states that the physician conducting the independent medical examination may ask the person being examined questions relating to their medical condition and medical history, but may not “interrogate” the person being examined.

Where, as in this case, the examination is to be a psychiatric one, it will obviously be necessary for the defendant's physician to ask the plaintiff many questions; this clinical examination is the primary way in which the physician will be able to acquire information about the plaintiff's psychiatric condition.

It is particularly important in this type of examination for a plaintiff to be assured, through the attendance of a physician of her choice, that the examination will be properly conducted and accurately reported.
The attendance of the plaintiff's nominee physician is therefore an integral step in the independent medical examination process. . . . . .
Where a party opposite wishes to have an independent medical examination, it must pay for all of the the costs associated with such an examination.

For example, it must pay the cost of the physician who will conduct the examination, of any nurse or other assistant who may be required, travel expenses for the party to be examined to attend the examination, the cost of equipment and tools used during the examination, the cost of the interpreter required to conduct the examination, etc.
Importantly, in the context of this application, the party must pay for the costs of the medical nominee of the party to be examined to attend the examination.
Morales v.
Seymour (1997), 52 Alta.
L.R.
117-18, per Veit J.
Mr.
Justice Lee would restrict Morales v.
Seymour (1997), 52 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 112 (Q.B.) to its own facts.
In Garrido v.
Pui (1998), 64 Alta.
L.R.
17, he said: I believe that the decision in Morales v.
Seymour, supra should be restricted to the unique fact situation that was before the Court.
In Pohynayko v.
Vries, 2001 ABCA 20, 2001 CarswellAlta 68, 277 A.R.
72, 94 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 288, Rooke J.
(ad hoc), at pp.
77-78, agreed that Morales v.
Seymour (1997), 52 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 112 (Q.B.) should be restricted to its unique facts.
The learned chambers justice noted that in Morales the plaintiff claimed impecuniosity and the cost of the attendance of the plaintiff's medical practitioner might be “quite high”.
He further noted that the plaintiff was Spanish speaking and needed an interpreter.
Finally, Lee J. seemed to accept the plaintiff's description of the role of the plaintiff medical practitioner in Morales, at p.

116: Not only will her psychiatrist protect her interests during the examination, and give her information as may be required during the course of the examination, but that physician will also be a witness, if necessary to what happened during the examination.

Lee J. then noted that in the application before him the plaintiff was not impecunious, the matter was a “relatively uncomplicated medical matter” (as opposed to the psychiatric issues involved in Morales), the medical practitioner was to have no special role in the examination, and the plaintiff had no language difficulties.
He then said at pp.
17-18: Based on these factual differences, there is a distinction therefore in the role of the medical nominee of the Plaintiff herein, and a question as to what purpose the medical nominee served.
There is no doubt that according to the Rule, the Plaintiff has a right to have a medical nominee attend at an independent medical examination requested by the Defendant.
However it seems that there should be some evidence as to the purpose or benefit gained by that attendance in order to saddle the Defendant with the costs of the medical nominee's presence. . . . . .
Even with respect to the Rule itself, it is silent as to who should bear the costs for the medical nominee.
Clearly, if Rule 217(5) had intended that the Defendant pay for the Plaintiff's medical nominee, the Rule could have so stated.

While the opposite conclusion is equally arguable, the non-specificity of the Rule in question here as to payment for the Plaintiff's medical nominee implies some sort of discretion, to be exercised judicially based on a concept such as “reasonableness”.

For example, the necessity, contribution of, or requirement for the Plaintiff's medical nominee would reasonably require compensation for the Plaintiff's medical nominee to be paid for by the Defendant.
The opposite result would occur in circumstances similar to the facts before me.
Generally, a litigant must pay for the cost of their [sic] own case.

While the Defendant is the party that requested the independent medical examination, and while the Plaintiff was entitled to have a nominee present during this independent medical examination, that does not necessarily mean that the Defendant must be responsible for the costs of the medial nominee.
There are many cases where legislation give [sic] parties rights but where the party exercising the benefit of that right invariably pays for the costs of exercising that right.

(ad hoc), speaking for the court, held that the costs associated with the nomination under Rule 217(5) of a medical practitioner to be present during the examination must be first borne by the party nominating the medical practitioner.
That party, if successful in the litigation then can seek to recover those costs.
At pp.
74-75, Rooke J. said: That rule 217(5) is a permissive right is unchallenged.
That is, it is the right of a party being examined by a medical practitioner to nominate another medical practitioner to attend the examination, without providing any other justification.
However, it is not a compulsory requirement.

The nomination of such a medical practitioner is not caused by an independent medical examination request by the defendant, but rather follows from it, as a discretionary right that may be exercised by the person to be examined, if so desired.
However, as to the costs of the nominee's attendance, it is, in substance, no different from other costs (mandatory or discretionary) that a plaintiff will incur in prosecuting an action.
In each case, as with other pretrial steps, the plaintiff would be required to pay the costs associated with such examinations and steps in the first instance.
A successful plaintiff can then apply for reimbursement of these costs at the end of the proceeding.
The same rules, in the normal case apply to the costs incurred by the plaintiff relating to the attendance of a nominee for a rule 217 examination.
It is to be noted that rule 217(2) provides that the “examination” is to be at the expense of the party seeking it.

It was conceded before us, and I concur, that that includes all of the costs necessary for the examination—obtaining the independent medical examiner, the reasonable transportation costs for the attendance of the party to be examined, and any ancillary tests that are done at the request of the defendant.
However, in my view, the attendance of the nominee is not necessary for the examination, but rather, as noted, is merely a discretionary right that the plaintiff may exercise.
Use of the video recording In Kohlendorfer v.

227, Justice Read discussed the use of video recordings of independent medical examinations.

5.43 which permits the defendant's expert to review the video recording before completing his or her report and which permits, as well, defendant's counsel to review the recording. … 38 In conclusion, the defendants in both these actions seek to permit the examiner who completed the DME to review the video recording of that DME before completing their report.
There is no valid reason for disabling them from doing so and many reasons to permit it.
There is also no valid reason to disable defence counsel from reviewing such video recordings and many good reasons to permit it, as outlined above.

Any other defence examiner whose examination is videotaped in these actions, should be permitted the same opportunity to review the video recordings of their examinations before completing their reports.

I do agree with the plaintiffs, however, that some limits are appropriate for video recordings.

Generally, there will be no reason to permit or require the defendant personally to view these recordings.

sentences.text: Conduct of examination

paragraphs.text: (1) A health care professional conducting a medical examination may ask the person being examined questions relating to that person's mental and physical condition and medical history, and the person being examined must answer the questions. (2) If the person to be examined agrees in writing, or if the Court so orders, the examining health care professional may (a) take or obtain samples from the person being examined, and make an analysis of the samples, and (b) perform any test recognized by medical science. (3) The party causing the medical examination to be conducted (a) must, on request, deliver promptly to each of the other parties a copy of a detailed written report of the health care professional's findings and conclusions, and (b) is, on request, entitled to receive promptly from the person examined a report of every medical examination previously or subsequently made of the physical or mental condition of the person resulting from the injuries sustained or the mental or physical condition that is in issue. (4) If a party refuses to provide a report in the manner described in subrule (3), the Court may order the report to be provided, and if the health care professional refuses to make the report in writing, the Court may make any order it considers proper, one of the provisions of which may be the exclusion of the health care professional's evidence if that person's evidence is offered at trial. (5) On application, the Court may make any order it considers necessary to limit or curtail a medical examination.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.44:1 Rule 5.44 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.44. 1. R. 5.44(5) applies to conduct, not recording, of examination In Nguyen v. Koehn, 2012 ABQB 655, 2012 CarswellAlta 1849, 550 A.R. 272, 77 Alta. L.R. (5th) 418, Madam Justice Moreau said, at paragraph 28: 28 Subrule 5.44(5) provides that, on application, the Court may make any order it considers necessary to limit or curtail a medical examination. I am of the view that this subrule pertains to the conduct of the medical examination itself, given the heading to Rule 5.44, which is “Conduct of examination,” and not to how the medical examination is recorded. The reference to “how the medical examination is recorded” related to the provisions in Rule 5.42 for the recording of the examination. 2. Court imposed limits on the examination In McElhone v. Indus School, 2019 ABCA 97, 2019 CarswellAlta 450, the plaintiff (a minor) was injured while at school, and commenced an action against the school and others. An application was brought for an order compelling an examination by a clinical psychologist. A Master ordered the examination, but restricted the testing to be conducted by the psychologist to testing as “agreed upon by the parties and without an interview”. No agreement was reached, and the matter was appealed to a Chambers Judge. The Chambers Judge “imposed limitations on the length of the interview, on two questions that the psychologist proposed to ask, and on the number of tests. She restricted the length of the assessment to seven hours, including a one-hour interview. The chambers judge permitted most of the proposed testing but concluded that four of the proposed tests could not be conducted and further that there could be no standard psychological tests unless agreed to by the respondent.” The appellants (the defendants) appealed the Chambers order on the grounds that it was an error to impose the limitations on the examination. The Court of Appeal agreed, and said: [8] This appeal is not about the threshold question of when a party can be examined by a health care professional under Rule 5.41(2). By the time this case reached the chambers judge the parties agreed that the respondent would attend at the medical examination. This appeal considers a different issue. Once the court has ordered the examination, what limits can be imposed on the health care professional, and what is the test for imposing such limits? [9] As a basic principle, health care professionals ought to have the ability to control their own examinations. Courts should be able to rely on the professional integrity and responsibilities of health care professionals, absent evidence which should override such trust. I agree with the comments of Acton J in Crone v Blue Cross Life Insurance Company of Canada, 2001 ABQB 787 (CanLII) at para 26, 297 AR 351: [I]t seems eminently reasonable that defence medical examiners, indeed all medical professionals, should be left to conduct their medical examinations as they see fit unless there is a compelling reason for the court to interfere or the rules permit it, as for example the rule allowing the presence of a medical nominee chosen by the plaintiff. The court cannot, in any event, compel a doctor to conduct an examination under circumstances which the doctor objects to, so if the courts begin to place constraints on how particular plaintiffs are examined, the predictable effect is that the number of doctors willing to perform defence medical examinations will decline, raising both the price and length of time to complete the discovery process in personal injury actions. [10] To similar effect is the comment of Read J in Feniak v Backhouse, 2010 ABQB 332 (CanLII), 534 AR 1, who observed that “[i]n the course of his or her examination, an examiner must be permitted to conduct such diagnostic tests as the examiner considers necessary in order to enable them to reach their conclusions and form their opinion”: at para 59. Although these cases were decided under the old Rule 217, the rationale remains sound. See also Wong v Wong, 2006 BCCA 540 (CanLII) at para 43, 227 DLR (4th) 220. [11] Given this rationale, what must the party seeking to limit the examination (who I will refer to as the plaintiff) establish and how does the plaintiff meet its onus? [12] The appellants submit that a plaintiff must establish a “real risk of substantial injury.” … [17] In my view a test that would require the plaintiff to establish a real risk of serious injury at the stage of imposing limits on the examination sets the bar too high. A more appropriate test is that the plaintiff must establish a compelling reason for limiting the test. This might include a risk of injury but could include other types of hardship. [18] For a reason to be compelling it must be examined in light of the purpose of Rules 5.41 to 5.44. The discovery provisions in Part 5 arise from the foundational principle that lawsuits should be decided on the merits. A party must disclose all relevant and material records and answer all relevant and material questions, whether helpful or unhelpful. There is no need to curtail an examination by limiting it to relevant and material questions, because that limit is implicit. In the context of an examination by a health care professional, a plaintiff cannot put her health in issue and then fail to disclose her medical condition. [19] With these principles in mind, a reason to limit an examination is compelling if the plaintiff's interest in maintaining the confidentiality of the information or otherwise curtailing the examination (a) significantly overrides the objectives of full pre-trial discovery, and (b) does not unfairly prevent the defendant from responding to the claim. [20] As the onus is on the party seeking to limit the examination, it is that party's obligation to adduce evidence in support of the need for limitations. This might include an affidavit of a medical professional or of the plaintiff, deposing to the circumstances which could justify the limitations. The burden could be met by presenting relevant evidence from a cross-examination of a proposed health care professional. … [22] The respondent is concerned about a particular question which the medical professional might ask. At the cross-examination on his affidavit, the psychologist was asked whether he would inquire of the respondent if she took birth control. He initially indicated that he would not, but then later stated that he might, as this could affect emotional functioning. Rule 5.44(1) provides that the medical professional may ask questions that relate to the plaintiff's medical and physical condition, including medical history and the plaintiff must answer the questions. In my view, and mindful of the fact that the psychologist is not yet familiar with the respondent, the court must rely upon the professional expertise and judgment of the expert as to whether he needs this information. Moreover, there is no evidence on the record to support any compelling reason to limit the question. Similar considerations apply to questions the psychologist suggested he might ask about the respondent's relationship with her twin sister. She has put that relationship in issue. It is not the court's role to second guess. … [24] It is important to note that there are other protections for a plaintiff who undergoes a medical examination. Rule 5.42(1) permits a plaintiff to nominate a health care professional to be present during the examination, to videotape the examination and to make a word-for-word recording of the examination. The chambers judge encouraged the plaintiff to make use of these protections. 3. Production of Non-Privileged Medical Reports Unaffected by Rule In Rosario-Paquet v. Hudec, 2000 ABQB 762, 2000 CarswellAlta 1247, 279 A.R. 319, the plaintiff's action arose out of a motor vehicle accident. When the plaintiff sought Section B insurance benefits, her insurer required her to undergo two medical examinations. She refused to produce for inspection the reports of those medical examinations (see R. 188), and the defendant sought an order compelling production for inspection under Rule 191. It was common ground that the Section B medical reports were not privileged. The plaintiff took the position that the defendant was not entitled to see the Section B medical reports until the defendant obtained and produced reports resulting from any rule 217 medical examination of the plaintiff. In ordering production for inspection of the Section B medical reports, Gallant J. said, at p. 323: It appears to me that it has always been the intention that rule 217 is to be utilized ordinarily only with respect to privileged medical evidence. On the plain wording of rule 187, it relates to all records of the party. On the plain wording of rule 191, which provides for an order for production, it must be intended to relate to all non-privileged documents. The defendant should not be required to resort to making an application under rule 209 to obtain the reports. If the drafters of the Rules of Court had intended that rules 187, 187.1 and 191 were to permit the plaintiff to withhold non-privileged medical reports until all rule 217 medical reports had been produced, they could easily have adjusted the wording of those Rules to so provide. Absent such qualification, a full literal interpretation should be given them. I respectfully disagree with the decision of Lefsrud, J., in [Soodhar v. Bagley (1999), 263 A.R. 119 (Q.B.)] that a defendant is entitled to receive Section B medical reports only upon delivery of his rule 217 reports to counsel for the plaintiff. 4. Plaintiff Must Also Produce Factual Underpinnings of Physician's Report In Andre v. Weibe, 2000 ABQB 946, 2000 CarswellAlta 1511, 284 A.R. 378, which was a personal injury action in which the plaintiff had been examined by two doctors, there was an application to produce the doctors' files including any notes, questionnaires, behavioural observations, and test score summary sheets. The application was granted. At pp. 380-381, Perras J. said: Rule 217(7) is a statutory exception to litigation privilege as it relates to expert reports sought by a defendant under rule 217. The rule mandates that such reports be disclosed to the plaintiff. The rule also mandates that these reports contain the “findings” made by the expert. “Findings” mean the factual underpinnings that support an expert's conclusions or opinions. … So, the test protocols and the raw data of test results arising from the examination would normally be the underpinnings that support an expert's conclusions and therefore should be disclosed. … At p. 382, His Lordship added: At this time, the Doctors need not disclose any documents which do not relate to the substance of their opinion (sic). For example, the Doctors need not disclose correspondence between themselves and the defendant, nor between themselves and counsel or agents for the defendant. Nor need they disclose any draft reports or any documents that describe the defendants' trial strategy. In Reid v. Bitangcol, 2016 ABQB 122, 2016 CarswellAlta 393, 36 Alta. L.R. (6th) 407, the Plaintiffs sued the Defendants alleging medical negligence in the treatment of a 16-year-old patient. The Plaintiffs served the Defendants with all the expert reports (“Plaintiffs' expert reports”) on which they intended to rely at trial. The Defendants applied for an order compelling production of the raw test data underlying the Plaintiffs' expert reports and a separate report (“the Michaels report”) referred to in the Plaintiffs' expert reports. In dismissing the application for the raw data, Justice Goss said: 18 I am not satisfied that the common law in Alberta supports the Defendants' application for disclosure of documents, test protocols and raw data from tests underlying the expert reports on which plaintiffs intend to rely for the completion of MEs under Rule 5.44. As stated in Erketu, disclosure of the plaintiffs' expert reports upon which they intend to rely at trial must occur first under Rule 5.35. However, this mandatory disclosure does not include disclosure of documents, test protocols and raw data from tests underlying the expert reports: Chernetz; Grammer. 19 A party delivering a detailed written report of the health care professional's findings and conclusions under Rule 5.44(3)(a) is entitled to receive, on request, every ME previously or subsequently made of the physical or mental condition of the person under Rule 5.44(3)(b). The continuing litigation privilege over related documents does not disappear until Rule 5.44(3) comes fully into play, in other words, when the reports under Rule 5.44(3)(a) have been provided, and a request has been made for Rule 5.44(3)(b) disclosure. In relation to the Michaels report, Justice Goss concluded: 25 In this case, the Plaintiffs' experts received a copy of the Michaels Report as part of the process of facilitating investigation and preparation of the Plaintiffs' case for trial, not to assess the Plaintiff pursuant to a statutorily determined process under the Minor Injury Regulation. I find that the Plaintiffs have not waived privilege through provision of the Michaels Report to their experts in the circumstances. In Alberta Drywall & Stucco Supply (Calgary) Inc. v. Alberta Drywall & Stucco Supply Inc., 2023 ABKB 696, the defendants applied for an order requiring the plaintiff to “provide the documents referred to by the expert in his report and used by the expert in preparing his report….In support of their application for production of records the defendants [submitted] that the plaintiff waived privilege over its expert's file when it filed the expert report and served it on the defendants.” Justice Dunlop said: [5] In support of their application for production of records the defendants submit that the plaintiff waived privilege over its expert's file when it filed the expert report and served it on the defendants. They rely on the recent decision of Ho v Connell, 2023 ABKB 133. [6] In Ho the defendants obtained a private investigator's report and provided it to a medical expert. The medical expert's report was disclosed to the plaintiff, but the private investigator's report was not. Feasby, J ordered that the private investigator's report be disclosed, holding that litigation privilege over that report had been waived by the combined effect of the investigator's report being provided to the medical expert and the medical expert's report being served on the plaintiff. The Court in Ho held that service of an expert's report waives privilege over the records the expert reviewed in forming his or her opinion, while acknowledging earlier decisions of this court which held the opposite, specifically Chernetz v Eagle Copters Ltd, 2005 ABQB 712, Grammer v Langpap, 2014 ABQB 74 and Reid v Bitangcol, 2016 ABQB 122. [7] There appear to be two lines of authority in Alberta, one which holds that privilege over an expert's report and the material the expert relied upon is not waived until the expert is called as a witness at trial and the other holding that privilege over those things is waived when one party serves the other with the expert's report, as is required for the expert to be called at trial, pursuant to r 5.35. …. [19] In my view, Stone [R. v. Stone [1999] 2 S.C.R. 290] stands for the principle that once a party has committed to calling an expert at trial, privilege over the expert's report is waived and the opposing party is entitled to the report and all foundational information. [20] In Ho, Feasby, J wrote: The right to question an expert in Rule 5.37, even though it is a contingent right, necessarily implies the right to explore the foundations of the expert's report. The waiver of privilege with respect to foundational information occurs when the expert report is exchanged because it is at that time when the party delivering the expert report signals to the other side its intention to rely at trial on the expert report and, by extension, the foundational information underlying the expert report. Ho at para 26 (emphasis added) [21] Rule 5.37 permits the court to order questioning of an expert only “in exceptional circumstances” and only where the expert is one a party is “proposing to call … at trial”. [22] With respect, I do not agree that by serving an expert report “the party delivering the expert report signals to the other side its intention to rely at trial on the expert report”. A party is free to not call an expert at trial whose report it previously served on the opposing party: Rances v Scaplen, 2008 ABQB 708 at para 219. All that a party serving an expert report does is keep its options open, to call or not call that expert. [23] I also do not agree that the possibility that pre-trial questioning of an expert may be ordered in exceptional cases results in a waiver of privilege over the foundational documents in every case. In my view, a better interpretation of r 5.37 is that production of the foundational documents may be ordered as a condition about questioning pursuant to r 5.37(3), as was done in BJM v SLM, 2012 ABQB 731 at para 36 – 37. [24] Obviously, serving an expert's report waives privilege over the report. In my view, it does not waive privilege over anything else. McMahon, J reached the same conclusion in Chernetz at para 12. [25] This is particularly important with respect to communications between a party or its principal and its own expert. Those communications are subject to litigation privilege and solicitor client privilege: Browne [Browne (Litigation Guardian of) v. Lavery [2002] O.J. No. 564] at para 30. 5. Obligation of Defendant The defendant must obtain a report in order to obtain the plaintiff's report. In Murphy v. Boully (1987), 50 Alta. L.R. (2d) 16 (Master), Master Quinn court held that a defendant must obtain an independent medical report on the plaintiff before he is entitled under R. 217 to receive copies of medical reports prepared by the plaintiff's medical examiners. At p. 18 he said: I must confess that I have some difficulty in understanding why a defendant must obtain an independent medical report on the plaintiff before he is entitled to receive production of the plaintiff's own medical report. In order to have access to the plaintiff's medical report the defendant must obtain an independent medical report on the plaintiff, even though he might not really want one. Rule 217, however, says what it says, and the decisions dealing with it indicate that it is interpreted to mean that a defendant must first obtain an independent medical report on the plaintiff. In Vokes v. Backer (1996), 45 Alta. L.R. (3d) 147 (Q.B.), a defendant sought a second medical examination of the plaintiff However, the defendant sought and obtained an order requiring the plaintiff to provide to the defendant certain reports from the plaintiff's medical experts before completion of the second medical examination. In setting aside that order, MacCallum J. said at p. 149: The difficulty is that the defendant demands these reports now before providing the report of his second [medical examination]. (B) The Rule says that the “examining health care professional” may take samples, and does not contemplate a third party such as a laboratory technician taking samples 9 This argument might be more compelling were it not for the fact that the Rule says “take or obtain”. It is hard to see how the court could make a meaningful order without requiring a person to attend for the taking of a sample. The appellant's affidavit states her belief that taking the test will cause her severe panic, stress and anxiety, and further her pain and suffering. Importantly, her affidavit does not say she is fearful of the knowledge that could result from the test, or discuss any possible psychological impact of such knowledge. 14 The courts must balance the interests of all the parties to the litigation. The possibility of Huntington's is not frivolous in this case, given the appellant's family history and the fact that several doctors have noted that she has symptoms consistent with that disease. If the blood test shows that to be a live possibility, it may indeed be relevant to assessing damages. Since the appellant has chosen to sue for damages, she cannot deprive the respondents from acquiring evidence that may assist in their defence.

5.44(5) applies to conduct, not recording, of examination In Nguyen v.
Koehn, 2012 ABQB 655, 2012 CarswellAlta 1849, 550 A.R.
L.R.
(5th) 418, Madam Justice Moreau said, at paragraph 28: 28 Subrule 5.44(5) provides that, on application, the Court may make any order it considers necessary to limit or curtail a medical examination.

I am of the view that this subrule pertains to the conduct of the medical examination itself, given the heading to Rule 5.44, which is “Conduct of examination,” and not to how the medical examination is recorded.
The reference to “how the medical examination is recorded” related to the provisions in Rule 5.42 for the recording of the examination.
Court imposed limits on the examination In McElhone v.
Indus School, 2019 ABCA 97, 2019 CarswellAlta 450, the plaintiff (a minor) was injured while at school, and commenced an action against the school and others.
An application was brought for an order compelling an examination by a clinical psychologist.
A Master ordered the examination, but restricted the testing to be conducted by the psychologist to testing as “agreed upon by the parties and without an interview”.
No agreement was reached, and the matter was appealed to a Chambers Judge.
The Chambers Judge “imposed limitations on the length of the interview, on two questions that the psychologist proposed to ask, and on the number of tests.
She restricted the length of the assessment to seven hours, including a one-hour interview.

The chambers judge permitted most of the proposed testing but concluded that four of the proposed tests could not be conducted and further that there could be no standard psychological tests unless agreed to by the respondent.” The appellants (the defendants) appealed the Chambers order on the grounds that it was an error to impose the limitations on the examination.
The Court of Appeal agreed, and said: [8] This appeal is not about the threshold question of when a party can be examined by a health care professional under Rule 5.41(2).
By the time this case reached the chambers judge the parties agreed that the respondent would attend at the medical examination.
This appeal considers a different issue.
Once the court has ordered the examination, what limits can be imposed on the health care professional, and what is the test for imposing such limits?
[9] As a basic principle, health care professionals ought to have the ability to control their own examinations.
Courts should be able to rely on the professional integrity and responsibilities of health care professionals, absent evidence which should override such trust.

I agree with the comments of Acton J in Crone v Blue Cross Life Insurance Company of Canada, 2001 ABQB 787 (CanLII) at para 26, 297 AR 351: [I]t seems eminently reasonable that defence medical examiners, indeed all medical professionals, should be left to conduct their medical examinations as they see fit unless there is a compelling reason for the court to interfere or the rules permit it, as for example the rule allowing the presence of a medical nominee chosen by the plaintiff.

The court cannot, in any event, compel a doctor to conduct an examination under circumstances which the doctor objects to, so if the courts begin to place constraints on how particular plaintiffs are examined, the predictable effect is that the number of doctors willing to perform defence medical examinations will decline, raising both the price and length of time to complete the discovery process in personal injury actions.

[10] To similar effect is the comment of Read J in Feniak v Backhouse, 2010 ABQB 332 (CanLII), 534 AR 1, who observed that “[i]n the course of his or her examination, an examiner must be permitted to conduct such diagnostic tests as the examiner considers necessary in order to enable them to reach their conclusions and form their opinion”: at para 59.
Although these cases were decided under the old Rule 217, the rationale remains sound.
See also Wong v Wong, 2006 BCCA 540 (CanLII) at para 43, 227 DLR (4th) 220.
[11] Given this rationale, what must the party seeking to limit the examination (who I will refer to as the plaintiff) establish and how does the plaintiff meet its onus?

[12] The appellants submit that a plaintiff must establish a “real risk of substantial injury.” … [17] In my view a test that would require the plaintiff to establish a real risk of serious injury at the stage of imposing limits on the examination sets the bar too high.
A more appropriate test is that the plaintiff must establish a compelling reason for limiting the test.
This might include a risk of injury but could include other types of hardship.
[18] For a reason to be compelling it must be examined in light of the purpose of Rules 5.41 to 5.44.
The discovery provisions in Part 5 arise from the foundational principle that lawsuits should be decided on the merits.
A party must disclose all relevant and material records and answer all relevant and material questions, whether helpful or unhelpful.
There is no need to curtail an examination by limiting it to relevant and material questions, because that limit is implicit.
In the context of an examination by a health care professional, a plaintiff cannot put her health in issue and then fail to disclose her medical condition.

[19] With these principles in mind, a reason to limit an examination is compelling if the plaintiff's interest in maintaining the confidentiality of the information or otherwise curtailing the examination
(a) significantly overrides the objectives of full pre-trial discovery, and
(b) does not unfairly prevent the defendant from responding to the claim.
[20] As the onus is on the party seeking to limit the examination, it is that party's obligation to adduce evidence in support of the need for limitations.
This might include an affidavit of a medical professional or of the plaintiff, deposing to the circumstances which could justify the limitations.

The burden could be met by presenting relevant evidence from a cross-examination of a proposed health care professional. … [22] The respondent is concerned about a particular question which the medical professional might ask.
At the cross-examination on his affidavit, the psychologist was asked whether he would inquire of the respondent if she took birth control.
He initially indicated that he would not, but then later stated that he might, as this could affect emotional functioning.

Rule 5.44(1) provides that the medical professional may ask questions that relate to the plaintiff's medical and physical condition, including medical history and the plaintiff must answer the questions.

In my view, and mindful of the fact that the psychologist is not yet familiar with the respondent, the court must rely upon the professional expertise and judgment of the expert as to whether he needs this information.
Moreover, there is no evidence on the record to support any compelling reason to limit the question.
Similar considerations apply to questions the psychologist suggested he might ask about the respondent's relationship with her twin sister.
She has put that relationship in issue.
It is not the court's role to second guess. … [24] It is important to note that there are other protections for a plaintiff who undergoes a medical examination.
Rule 5.42(1) permits a plaintiff to nominate a health care professional to be present during the examination, to videotape the examination and to make a word-for-word recording of the examination.
The chambers judge encouraged the plaintiff to make use of these protections.
Production of Non-Privileged Medical Reports Unaffected by Rule In Rosario-Paquet v.
Hudec, 2000 ABQB 762, 2000 CarswellAlta 1247, 279 A.R.
319, the plaintiff's action arose out of a motor vehicle accident.
When the plaintiff sought Section B insurance benefits, her insurer required her to undergo two medical examinations.
She refused to produce for inspection the reports of those medical examinations (see R.
188), and the defendant sought an order compelling production for inspection under Rule 191.
It was common ground that the Section B medical reports were not privileged.

The plaintiff took the position that the defendant was not entitled to see the Section B medical reports until the defendant obtained and produced reports resulting from any rule 217 medical examination of the plaintiff.
In ordering production for inspection of the Section B medical reports, Gallant J. said, at p.
323: It appears to me that it has always been the intention that rule 217 is to be utilized ordinarily only with respect to privileged medical evidence.
On the plain wording of rule 187, it relates to all records of the party.
On the plain wording of rule 191, which provides for an order for production, it must be intended to relate to all non-privileged documents.
The defendant should not be required to resort to making an application under rule 209 to obtain the reports.

If the drafters of the Rules of Court had intended that rules 187, 187.1 and 191 were to permit the plaintiff to withhold non-privileged medical reports until all rule 217 medical reports had been produced, they could easily have adjusted the wording of those Rules to so provide.
Absent such qualification, a full literal interpretation should be given them.
I respectfully disagree with the decision of Lefsrud, J., in [Soodhar v.
Bagley (1999), 263 A.R.
119 (Q.B.)] that a defendant is entitled to receive Section B medical reports only upon delivery of his rule 217 reports to counsel for the plaintiff.
Plaintiff Must Also Produce Factual Underpinnings of Physician's Report In Andre v.
Weibe, 2000 ABQB 946, 2000 CarswellAlta 1511, 284 A.R.

378, which was a personal injury action in which the plaintiff had been examined by two doctors, there was an application to produce the doctors' files including any notes, questionnaires, behavioural observations, and test score summary sheets.
The application was granted.
At pp.
380-381, Perras J. said: Rule 217(7) is a statutory exception to litigation privilege as it relates to expert reports sought by a defendant under rule 217.
The rule mandates that such reports be disclosed to the plaintiff.

The rule also mandates that these reports contain the “findings” made by the expert. “Findings” mean the factual underpinnings that support an expert's conclusions or opinions. … So, the test protocols and the raw data of test results arising from the examination would normally be the underpinnings that support an expert's conclusions and therefore should be disclosed. … At p.
382, His Lordship added: At this time, the Doctors need not disclose any documents which do not relate to the substance of their opinion (sic).
For example, the Doctors need not disclose correspondence between themselves and the defendant, nor between themselves and counsel or agents for the defendant.
Nor need they disclose any draft reports or any documents that describe the defendants' trial strategy.
In Reid v.
Bitangcol, 2016 ABQB 122, 2016 CarswellAlta 393, 36 Alta.
L.R.
(6th) 407, the Plaintiffs sued the Defendants alleging medical negligence in the treatment of a 16-year-old patient.
The Plaintiffs served the Defendants with all the expert reports (“Plaintiffs' expert reports”) on which they intended to rely at trial.

The Defendants applied for an order compelling production of the raw test data underlying the Plaintiffs' expert reports and a separate report (“the Michaels report”) referred to in the Plaintiffs' expert reports.

In dismissing the application for the raw data, Justice Goss said: 18 I am not satisfied that the common law in Alberta supports the Defendants' application for disclosure of documents, test protocols and raw data from tests underlying the expert reports on which plaintiffs intend to rely for the completion of MEs under Rule 5.44.
As stated in Erketu, disclosure of the plaintiffs' expert reports upon which they intend to rely at trial must occur first under Rule 5.35.
However, this mandatory disclosure does not include disclosure of documents, test protocols and raw data from tests underlying the expert reports: Chernetz; Grammer.

19 A party delivering a detailed written report of the health care professional's findings and conclusions under Rule 5.44(3)(a) is entitled to receive, on request, every ME previously or subsequently made of the physical or mental condition of the person under Rule 5.44(3)(b).

The continuing litigation privilege over related documents does not disappear until Rule 5.44(3) comes fully into play, in other words, when the reports under Rule 5.44(3)(a) have been provided, and a request has been made for Rule 5.44(3)(b) disclosure.

In relation to the Michaels report, Justice Goss concluded: 25 In this case, the Plaintiffs' experts received a copy of the Michaels Report as part of the process of facilitating investigation and preparation of the Plaintiffs' case for trial, not to assess the Plaintiff pursuant to a statutorily determined process under the Minor Injury Regulation.
I find that the Plaintiffs have not waived privilege through provision of the Michaels Report to their experts in the circumstances.
In Alberta Drywall & Stucco Supply (Calgary) Inc. v.

Alberta Drywall & Stucco Supply Inc., 2023 ABKB 696, the defendants applied for an order requiring the plaintiff to “provide the documents referred to by the expert in his report and used by the expert in preparing his report….In support of their application for production of records the defendants [submitted] that the plaintiff waived privilege over its expert's file when it filed the expert report and served it on the defendants.” Justice Dunlop said: [5] In support of their application for production of records the defendants submit that the plaintiff waived privilege over its expert's file when it filed the expert report and served it on the defendants.
They rely on the recent decision of Ho v Connell, 2023 ABKB 133.
[6] In Ho the defendants obtained a private investigator's report and provided it to a medical expert.
The medical expert's report was disclosed to the plaintiff, but the private investigator's report was not.

Feasby, J ordered that the private investigator's report be disclosed, holding that litigation privilege over that report had been waived by the combined effect of the investigator's report being provided to the medical expert and the medical expert's report being served on the plaintiff.

The Court in Ho held that service of an expert's report waives privilege over the records the expert reviewed in forming his or her opinion, while acknowledging earlier decisions of this court which held the opposite, specifically Chernetz v Eagle Copters Ltd, 2005 ABQB 712, Grammer v Langpap, 2014 ABQB 74 and Reid v Bitangcol, 2016 ABQB 122.

[7] There appear to be two lines of authority in Alberta, one which holds that privilege over an expert's report and the material the expert relied upon is not waived until the expert is called as a witness at trial and the other holding that privilege over those things is waived when one party serves the other with the expert's report, as is required for the expert to be called at trial, pursuant to r 5.35. ….
[19] In my view, Stone [R. v.
Stone [1999] 2 S.C.R.

290] stands for the principle that once a party has committed to calling an expert at trial, privilege over the expert's report is waived and the opposing party is entitled to the report and all foundational information.
[20] In Ho, Feasby, J wrote: The right to question an expert in Rule 5.37, even though it is a contingent right, necessarily implies the right to explore the foundations of the expert's report.

The waiver of privilege with respect to foundational information occurs when the expert report is exchanged because it is at that time when the party delivering the expert report signals to the other side its intention to rely at trial on the expert report and, by extension, the foundational information underlying the expert report.

Ho at para 26 (emphasis added) [21] Rule 5.37 permits the court to order questioning of an expert only “in exceptional circumstances” and only where the expert is one a party is “proposing to call … at trial”.
[22] With respect, I do not agree that by serving an expert report “the party delivering the expert report signals to the other side its intention to rely at trial on the expert report”.
A party is free to not call an expert at trial whose report it previously served on the opposing party: Rances v Scaplen, 2008 ABQB 708 at para 219.
All that a party serving an expert report does is keep its options open, to call or not call that expert.

[23] I also do not agree that the possibility that pre-trial questioning of an expert may be ordered in exceptional cases results in a waiver of privilege over the foundational documents in every case.

In my view, a better interpretation of r 5.37 is that production of the foundational documents may be ordered as a condition about questioning pursuant to r 5.37(3), as was done in BJM v SLM, 2012 ABQB 731 at para 36 – 37.
[24] Obviously, serving an expert's report waives privilege over the report.
In my view, it does not waive privilege over anything else.
McMahon, J reached the same conclusion in Chernetz at para 12.
[25] This is particularly important with respect to communications between a party or its principal and its own expert.
Those communications are subject to litigation privilege and solicitor client privilege: Browne [Browne (Litigation Guardian of) v.
Lavery [2002] O.J.
No.
564] at para 30.
Obligation of Defendant The defendant must obtain a report in order to obtain the plaintiff's report.
In Murphy v.
Boully (1987), 50 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 16 (Master), Master Quinn court held that a defendant must obtain an independent medical report on the plaintiff before he is entitled under R.
217 to receive copies of medical reports prepared by the plaintiff's medical examiners.
At p.

In order to have access to the plaintiff's medical report the defendant must obtain an independent medical report on the plaintiff, even though he might not really want one.
Rule 217, however, says what it says, and the decisions dealing with it indicate that it is interpreted to mean that a defendant must first obtain an independent medical report on the plaintiff.

L.R.

(3d) 147 (Q.B.), a defendant sought a second medical examination of the plaintiff However, the defendant sought and obtained an order requiring the plaintiff to provide to the defendant certain reports from the plaintiff's medical experts before completion of the second medical examination.

He says that he needs to see the reports before even choosing his second expert because the contents of the report will assist in the choice of the expert.
